_note: The public what's-new feed, rendered at the bottom of the Methodology page. Committed rather than built: web/data/ is generated and gitignored, and this is a written record, not an output. NEWEST FIRST. `kind` is one of ship (a feature), model (the numbers changed), fix (something was wrong), or refuse (something was measured and deliberately not built) — the last one matters as much as the first three, because a decision nobody wrote down gets re-made by somebody who has not seen the reasoning. A `model` entry must name what moved on the board; see engine/ledger.MODEL_ERAS, which the same page renders beside these with the results each era actually produced.

entries.title: Every finished game lists the parlays the Record counts
entries.body: On Report Picks' “How our reports did”, last week's Thursday and Sunday NFL games showed their picks but none of their parlays, though the Record counted them. Every finished game now lists the same parlays the Record counts, each one won or lost, and a game with no picks or parlays says why.

entries.title: Finished college basketball games keep their scan
entries.body: Once the night's last college basketball game tipped off, every finished game's page lost its Matchup scan and Team shapes radar. They now stay up, as they do for the NBA.

entries.title: College football's full matchup scan reaches more schools
entries.body: About 30 college football schools, including several in the MAC, weren't being matched to the advanced stats our college matchup scan and team ratings use. They are now, so more college games get the full scan with its players who could shine or struggle.

entries.title: College football moneylines on game pages
entries.body: College football game pages showed a dash for the moneyline on every game. They now show both teams' prices, and college games get the same opening line, line movement and closing line as the other leagues.

entries.title: Road favorites' spreads stored the right way round
entries.body: In every league but the NFL, a game where the road team was favored had its spread saved the wrong way round, which threw off the closing-line numbers the Record shows for spread bets and the line-movement notes on game pages. That's fixed, the saved lines are corrected, and every finished game's page now shows its closing line.

entries.title: Team shapes on college game pages
entries.body: College football and college basketball game pages now show the Team shapes radar too, ranked only against the schools in their own division, so a lopsided game against a smaller school doesn't skew anyone's shape.

entries.title: Team shapes on NBA, WNBA and hockey game pages
entries.body: The Team shapes radar from the NFL's game pages (each team's scoring, defense, recent form, home edge and steadiness against the rest of its league) is now on NBA, WNBA and hockey game pages too.

entries.title: College football game pages get the Matchup scan
entries.body: Every college football game page now has the Matchup scan the other sports' game pages have: each team's points, passing and rushing yards for and against, yards a carry and a pass, and interceptions, ranked among the FBS teams, with the points the lines expect and the key matchups, from our own box scores.

entries.title: College football injuries from the schools' own reports
entries.body: College football now reads the Big Ten's, SEC's, ACC's and Big 12's availability reports for every conference game, the evenings before and on game day. A school's newest word replaces ESPN's older one on the Injuries page, in the game reports and in the picks, and a player the school lists as available is cleared. A game between two of those schools now posts its picks and parlays once both game-day reports are in, 50 minutes before kickoff at the latest.

entries.title: No years-old injury lines
entries.body: College football's Injuries page showed one player as out with "filed Nov 21": the line was from November 2020, and ESPN had never removed it. Any injury filed more than a year ago now comes off the Injuries page and out of what our picks read, and an older filing shows its year.

entries.title: Every sport's big plays are titled the same way
entries.body: In the Live tab's Play feed and the game chats, a basketball play read "Coby White — Jump Shot" even when it was a three, and a hockey play "NJD Goal — Nico Hischier", while football's read "CIN Pass intercepted" with the player underneath. Every sport's play now says its team and what happened ("MEM Three-pointer", "NJD Goal"), with each player on a line of their own, and a shared play or a thread says whose it was.

entries.title: Basketball's and hockey's live cards say each play as a sentence
entries.body: On the Live tab, NBA, WNBA, college basketball and hockey cards listed each play as a label, like "MEM · Zach Edey — Defensive Rebound". They now say it as the game page and football's cards do: "Coby White makes a 3-point running jump shot, assist Brandon Miller", "Connor Brown shoots, saved by Cam Talbot". New Orleans players also get their club's logo on the game page.

entries.title: Spreads say who gives the points in every league
entries.body: On the Live tab, the side rail and the game pages, an NBA, hockey or college game with the away team favoured showed the spread backwards (Memphis +2.5 beside Memphis -145). Every league's spread now reads the right way round, and the line chip on the game page and the team page now names the favourite in every league, not only the NFL.

entries.title: College basketball's live plays read in words
entries.body: The Live tab's college basketball cards showed the feed's codes, like "LayUpShot" and "MadeFreeThrow miss". They now read as the NBA's do ("Layup", "Free Throw"), and a card's few rows are plays: substitutions and dead-ball rebounds stay on the game's own page.

entries.title: No breakout candidate our own pick bets against
entries.body: A game report no longer lists a player as a breakout candidate (or a fade) when our own pick on him goes the other way. His card now says both sides plainly and calls it mixed, and the pick stays as it was.

entries.title: "Spot" or "matchup", said the same way in every league
entries.body: A player's verdict now says "good spot" or "tough spot" when it comes from the night itself (a back-to-back, a likely blowout, the points the lines expect, his own role) rather than from the opponent, in the NBA, WNBA, college basketball, hockey and baseball, the way football's reports already do. "Matchup" is kept for verdicts the opponent's defense, goalie or starting pitcher actually decided.

entries.title: NBA chances that say what the picks win
entries.body: Our NBA Most Likely picks have been winning more often than the chance we showed. Where our number and the betting price agree on a pick, the chance shown now comes from how often picks like it have actually won, which can be higher than both. It switches on by itself once it proves more accurate on games it never learned from, and off again if it stops; on the record so far it is close but not there yet. Once on, it moves the NBA's chances, tiers and order on Most Likely, not which picks are listed. Hockey gets it only if its own record shows the same, and so far it does not.

entries.title: Game reports stop arguing with themselves
entries.body: A player's matchup verdict no longer points against the defense numbers printed beside it. When the numbers disagree, the card says so and leans neither way. When the verdict comes from the weather or the betting lines rather than the defense, it says "tough spot" or "favorable spot" instead of blaming the defense. Receiver and tight end cards also say which defense number our projections use.

entries.title: Season averages count the right games
entries.body: A player's season line divided every stat by every game, even games whose box score did not have that stat yet, so a WNBA star could read 113% from three. Averages now count only the games that have each stat, and percentages only the games with both made and attempted.

entries.title: Team rosters read like the player pages
entries.body: Every team page's roster now gives height and weight one way, 6'2" and 190 lb, in every league, as the player pages do. College and basketball rosters used to read 6' 1" and 214 lbs.

entries.title: The tab you just tapped stays readable
entries.body: On a phone, the sub-tab you had just tapped turned dark grey with dark writing until you tapped somewhere else. It now stays gold with dark writing, on every page with sub-tabs.

entries.title: SGPX parlays for college football
entries.body: College football now gets SGPX tickets too: our strongest college picks from different games in the same kickoff window, three player-prop and three touchdown tickets a window, and day tickets across the day's windows. A window's tickets post once its games have posted their own picks, 90 minutes before kickoff, and never change.

entries.title: SGPX parlays, live
entries.body: Once a game on an SGPX ticket starts, the Live tab follows the ticket leg by leg, each leg with its own game and its number so far, like the game report parlays.

entries.title: SGPX day parlays
entries.body: A day with more than one kickoff window now also gets SGPX tickets that join our best picks from different windows, posted with the day's first games. Every SGPX ticket now names the one sportsbook that has every leg, and they are listed on Report Picks beside the game report picks and on Best Parlays in their own tab.

entries.title: Players back with their old team
entries.body: When a new starting quarterback is back with a team he used to start for, like Kirk Cousins with the Vikings, his game report now says how he played there: his starts, his yards and touchdowns a game, and how much of his targets went to each receiver still on the team. A receiver, tight end or running back back with an old team gets his catches, yards and carries a game from his time there.

entries.title: SGPX parlays
entries.body: Our strongest NFL picks from different games in the same kickoff window, combined into one ticket: three player-prop tickets and three touchdown tickets a window, each with our chance and the price to take it at. They post once every game in the window has posted its picks, and they are on each game report, on Report Picks in their own tab, and graded on the Record.

entries.title: NFL inactives, checked every minute
entries.body: In the 100 minutes before an NFL kickoff, the site now checks ESPN's injury board every minute instead of every ten, and a game's picks post as soon as both teams' inactives are in instead of at the next scheduled rebuild.

entries.title: Moved NFL games keep the right kickoff
entries.body: When the NFL moves a game to another time slot and our schedule has not caught up, the site now takes the game's time from ESPN's live scoreboard, so its picks, parlays and inactives are timed to the real kickoff.

entries.title: Baseball team pages open again
entries.body: Every MLB team page timed out before it loaded. They now open quickly: the season's stats are read once for every team and kept until a stat line changes.

entries.title: Settled parlays, leg by leg
entries.body: A finished game's parlays now show each leg in its own box, green if it won and red if it lost, with what the player did and the final score under it, and the whole parlay outlined green if it won and red if it lost. The game report, Report Picks and the Record all show them this way.

entries.title: NFL picks wait for the inactives
entries.body: An NFL game's picks and parlays now post once both teams' inactives are in, 75 minutes before kickoff when they are, and 50 minutes before at the latest, so the posted picks know who is playing.

entries.title: Active after the inactives
entries.body: Once an NFL team's game-day inactives are out, a player still listed questionable who is not on the list is treated as playing: his own props can be picked, and his game's report says he is active.

entries.title: A new quarterback's own favorite targets
entries.body: When a backup quarterback starts, his receivers', tight ends' and backs' numbers now lean toward who he has thrown to in his own starts, as measured on ten NFL seasons. A quarterback's "chemistry" with one particular receiver did not predict anything, so it is not used.

entries.title: The newest injury word, everywhere
entries.body: When the latest report on a listed player says he is expected to play, or to miss the game, the Injuries page and every game report's injury lines now say so, with who reported it, even while his listing still says questionable.

entries.title: Five WNBA team pages fill in
entries.body: The Aces', Valkyries', Sparks', Liberty's and Mystics' team pages showed a bare team code with no roster or depth chart. They now show the full name, the roster and the depth chart like every other club.

entries.title: The Injuries page says probable or questionable
entries.body: Under ESPN's "Day-To-Day", the Injuries page now shows an NBA player's official word for today's or tomorrow's game when the injury report gives it, like "questionable for Sun".

entries.title: All-Star games out of basketball players' seasons
entries.body: NBA and WNBA player pages counted All-Star games and exhibitions against national teams as games of the season, and their averages with them. The site now takes those games out of its stored history every night, along with older seasons' preseason games.

entries.title: Probable, questionable or doubtful, not just day-to-day
entries.body: ESPN lists every NBA player who might miss a game as day-to-day. Our NBA game reports now say the league's own word for the game when the injury report gives it: probable, questionable or doubtful.

entries.title: The newest word on a listed player
entries.body: When a player listed questionable or day-to-day gets new word that he will play, or will miss the game, his game's page now says so, with who reported it, even before his listing changes. Every league's game reports.

entries.title: If the quarterback plays, and if he sits
entries.body: When a starting quarterback is questionable or a game-time decision, his game's report now shows both versions, right under our picks: who starts if he sits, what that has done to his receivers before, and how each of his team's numbers moves either way. Our picks still post once, after the inactives, from the version that holds. NFL and college football.

entries.title: Most Likely, Report Picks and Best Parlays, one switch
entries.body: The Picks button still opens Most Likely. At the top of Most Likely, Report Picks and Best Parlays there is now one switch between the three, so the game reports' picks and parlays are a tap away from the Most Likely picks, and the Picks button stays lit on all three.

entries.title: Game report picks post once, then never change
entries.body: A report used to choose its picks again every few minutes, so a game piled up picks during the day and you could see different ones each visit. Now a game's picks post once, with its parlays: 75 minutes before an NFL kickoff and 90 minutes before other games, from the newest injury news and lines. Until then the report says when they post; after, they stay exactly as posted, and they are the ones the Record counts.

entries.title: WNBA player pages fill in every box-score column
entries.body: WNBA player pages showed minutes, points, rebounds and assists only, where NBA pages show steals, blocks, turnovers and shooting too: the WNBA's games were filed before we kept those columns. Each night now reads a batch of those games again, so the pages fill in over the coming nights.

entries.title: Hockey and college basketball Record pages work like the NFL's
entries.body: These two leagues stake nothing yet, so their Record leads with the Most Likely record, but the page under it read an empty one: greyed 90, 30 and 7-day buttons, a verdict of 0-0-0 and “too early to read (0 of 30)”. The buttons, the verdict, the running profit chart and the splits now read the record at the top of the page, as the NFL's page does.

entries.title: A finished game reads Final on its page
entries.body: A basketball game that ended between two of the live scoreboard's updates could still read LIVE on its page the next morning, with its last plays missing. Its page now reads Final with every play, and every finished game's page says the day it was played, as the NFL's already did, where some said “updated 10 hr ago”.

entries.title: Player pages read the same in every sport
entries.body: Every player page now says height and weight one way (6'2", 190 lb), college and baseball pages show the size, class and hometown their rosters give, a college player's previous game counts each game once (Ohio State read 15-9), the WNBA's Aces, Liberty, Valkyries, Sparks and Mystics are named on every player page, and a shooting percentage no longer shows up as a count.

entries.title: No more “NaN°F” on a game page
entries.body: A game with no weather on file read “NaN°F · NaNmph · kickoff forecast” at the top of its page. It now says “Outdoor · weather not pulled”, as the game cards already did.

entries.title: Game reports show exactly the parlays that post
entries.body: Each game report wrote its own copy of the game's parlays a moment before the post time and the lock were applied, so a report could show parlays before they posted, and after they posted, each newest build's set instead of the locked one that Report Picks, Best Parlays and the Record use. Now a report shows exactly what posts: before the post time it says when its parlays post, and after, the posted set, unchanged.

entries.title: NBA parlays: one leg on at most two of a game's parlays
entries.body: A leg could ride four of an NBA game's six parlays, so one miss could sink most of them: on our graded NBA tickets, four legs that each rode four tickets lost and took 16 tickets with them. Now a leg rides at most two of a game's two-leg and three-leg parlays together. How often a ticket hits is unchanged; one miss no longer sinks most of a game's parlays. A game with few strong legs may post fewer two-leg parlays, and says why.

entries.title: Parlay post times read in your own time zone
entries.body: Each game's parlays post shortly before it starts. Its report now says when in your own time zone, as every start on the site does, and Best Parlays gives the day of the next post when it is not today.

entries.title: Game report parlays post shortly before each game, then never change
entries.body: On our record, the final parlays a game report carried at game time hit far more than the earlier versions it replaced during the day (three-leg 36% against 26%, touchdown and goal-scorer pairs 18% against 7%), because they knew the day's injury news, lineups and line moves. Now each game's parlays post once, 90 minutes before it starts (75 for the NFL, just after inactives), built from the newest numbers, and never change. What you bet is the set the Record counts.

entries.title: Best Parlays, one tap from Report Picks
entries.body: Best Parlays ranks every parlay the game reports posted, best to worst, with a Two-leg and a Three-leg switch, the way Most Likely ranks picks. Report Picks now opens it from a button at the top of its Today's picks tab.

entries.title: A posted parlay never changes, and the Record shows every one we posted
entries.body: A game report's parlays could change during the day as numbers and news moved, so a parlay you bet in the morning could be gone by game time, and the Record counted only the set at the start. Now, in every sport, once a parlay is posted it stays exactly as posted until the game: same players, lines and prices. For past games, the Record adds a line for every parlay we posted, including the ones replaced before their game, and each finished game lists those replaced versions, each marked hit or missed.

entries.title: Best Parlays' Top tier fills again in the NFL, college football and the NBA
entries.body: Since this afternoon's change that holds each parlay leg to the sportsbook's own chance, one Best Parlays check (whether a book's same-game price pays enough) could not pass in those leagues, so no player-prop parlay there ranked as a Top parlay. That check now stays silent where legs are held to the book's chance, as the Safe and Balanced labels already do. Which parlays are built is unchanged.

entries.title: Hockey's live page draws the win chance line
entries.body: Every sport's live game page shows a line of each side's win chance through the game, except hockey, where the feed gives no chance after each play, so it showed only today's number as two bars. Hockey now draws the same line from our own reading of the score and the clock at each play, marked as ours, ending on the live score.

entries.title: No new rules for five football prop types
entries.body: College passing-yards overs, college rushing- and receiving-yards unders and NFL rushing attempts have hit well under what we said. We measured a rule to keep them off parlays and found they have nearly left the board already: since Nov 15 the NFL's 60% bar and college's bar and price hold leave 0 to 5 of each. College passing overs' slump came from two Saturdays when every passing over missed and the books' prices missed it too, so a rule would chase noise.

entries.title: Football kickoff times in your own time zone
entries.body: NFL kickoff times always showed Eastern time, even if you picked another time zone in Settings. They now show in your zone wherever a game's start appears: game cards and pages, the next-kickoff line, a player's next game, the inactives note and the parlay grader, which now shows college football start times too. The next-kickoff line also picks the earliest game by its real time.

entries.title: The Record grades Best Parlays by tier
entries.body: Each league's parlay record on the Record page now says how Top parlays, Strong and Worth a look tickets have done, by the tier each ticket had when its game started, with the chance we gave them. Games from before the Best Parlays page went up are tiered by the same checks.

entries.title: College football's Thursday-night games are featured
entries.body: Like the NFL's Thursday and Monday night games and Lions games, a college football game kicking off on a Thursday night now gets a deeper report card (six picks instead of four), a badge with how games like it have done, and a record of its own.

entries.title: NFL pass attempts benched; NFL picks far above their price capped
entries.body: NFL quarterback pass-attempt picks are no longer staked and ride no parlay: on our record they lost on both sides (Edge picks 21-26, -4.0 units). And an NFL Most Likely pick is now shown at no more than ten points above its price's chance: picks shown further above it hit 47% where we said 79%. On the board those picks show the lower chance and sit lower.

entries.title: The parlay record's book chances read each leg's own line
entries.body: The Record page's parlay legs show the sportsbook's own chance beside ours. For picks on alternate lines that was the main line's chance, so the book's numbers read 7 to 10 points low (the NBA's 53% where its legs were priced near 63%). New legs now record their own line's chance, and the Record shows it. The correction each league learns for its parlay legs switches to it only when its own record shows that scores better.

entries.title: Alternate-line picks read at their own line's chance
entries.body: This afternoon's change that holds each parlay leg to the sportsbook's own chance read the wrong number for picks on alternate lines: it used the main line's chance (about 50% at -110) instead of the alternate line's own (about 67% at -250). Most NFL legs fell under the 60% a leg needs, and NFL reports posted 6 player-prop parlays where that morning's had posted 60. The report cards made the same mistake and moved those picks behind touchdown picks. Both now read each pick's own line, as the evidence for the rule was measured.

entries.title: Game report picks, live
entries.body: The Live tab now follows every game report's picks while their games are played, the way it follows the Edge and Most Likely bets: a panel of their own with each pick's number so far, what it still needs and whether it has cleared, and where the report posted it. Each game's page lists them on its picks rail above the report's parlays, which the Live tab already followed leg by leg. For members.

entries.title: NBA parlays are labeled Safe and Balanced again
entries.body: Since NBA parlay legs started counting at the lower of our chance and the sportsbook's, almost no leg could show as a better price than the book's, and the Safe and Balanced labels need such legs, so nearly every NBA parlay would have read Pop or Long shot. NBA labels now go by the legs' chances alone, as football's do. Hockey's labels are unchanged.

entries.title: Quarterback pass-attempt overs leave football's parlays
entries.body: An NFL quarterback's pass-attempt over no longer rides a game report's parlays, and it goes behind the other picks on a report's card. On our record those legs hit 20 of 41 where we and the sportsbook both said about two in three, while every other NFL leg rated as high hit 65-68%. Completions, the same kind of bet, were already benched. The picks stay on the board.

entries.title: Touchdown pairs lead with two scorers at 40%
entries.body: A football game report's two-leg touchdown pairs now put first the pairs whose two scorers we both rate 40% or better to score. On our record those scorers found the end zone 46-58% of the time, against 36-44% for the rest; in college two of them landed together about 27% of the time, two under the line about 15%. The research behind each scorer still orders the pairs on either side of that line. A shorter-priced pair pays less; the point is that it lands more often.

entries.title: Report cards lead with the picks the record backs
entries.body: A game report's card now puts two kinds of pick behind the rest: an NFL pick whose chance sits far above the sportsbook's own (those hit 45-53% on our record where we said 75-87%, against 58% for every other NFL pick), and an NBA prop a single play settles (62% as a single against 65% for the rest). They stay on the board; they just no longer take a card's top places.

entries.title: Fantasy points are back on football game pages
entries.body: The game's top fantasy scorers so far, in PPR and half-PPR from its box score, had dropped off NFL and college football game pages when the page was redesigned. They are a card again on the Stats tab, under the box scores.

entries.title: Parlay legs the market backs
entries.body: In the NFL, college football and the NBA a parlay leg now counts at the lower of our chance and the sportsbook's own. On our record, football legs we rated 60% or better at prices near even money hit about 40-50%, while legs the market also rates that likely hit what we said, so a ticket is now built only from legs both agree on, and its chance is honest. NBA props a single play settles (over 1.5 rebounds, over 0.5 threes, under 0.5 blocks) stay on the board as picks but no longer ride a parlay: they hit 62% where every other leg we rated as high hit 68%. Hockey's parlays, which beat their numbers, are unchanged.

entries.title: Best Parlays: every report parlay, ranked best to worst
entries.body: A new page ranks every parlay the game reports post across a league's games, the way Most Likely ranks a pick: Top parlays, Strong and Worth a look by how many of a ticket's checks it passes, then our chance of the whole ticket. Player-prop parlays (two-leg and three-leg, each ranked on its own) and touchdown pairs (goal scorers in hockey) each have a section of their own. Each card shows the legs with their prices, our chance, the one book that has the whole ticket and what keeps it out of the tier above, with a Bet it button that puts the ticket on that book's slip. Members only.

entries.title: Baseball's game page matches every other sport's
entries.body: A baseball game opens on the same page as every other sport: the score on the two clubs' colours with the bases, outs and count, a bar that keeps it in view, the line score by inning, the ballpark with who is up and every pitch of the at-bat, the last at-bat said in a sentence with the batter's and pitcher's lines, the at-bats an inning at a time, team stats, both box scores, standings and our picks.

entries.title: Parlays a single sportsbook can place, and stricter college picks
entries.body: Each game's parlays now favor ones a single sportsbook prices whole, since a same-game parlay is placed at one book. College football picks ask 60%, as the NFL's do, and a college pass catcher's picks follow the NFL's rule behind a new quarterback too green to rate. In football a receiver's coverage matchup explains his pick but no longer lifts it; only the measured matchup effect does. In the NBA and the NHL our record may now raise a chance toward its price where picks have beaten what we said. Saturday's college games are priced from Friday, so their reports carry picks and parlays a day early.

entries.title: Every sport's live game page now matches the NFL's
entries.body: A basketball or hockey game opens on the same page a football game does: the score on the two clubs' colours, a bar that keeps the score in view when you scroll, the line score, the last play said in a sentence with the players in it, the win chance, the game chat, and four tabs: Stats, Play-By-Play, Standings and Our picks. The court and the rink sit where football has its field, with the same views as before. Plays read as sentences, a period to a card, with the one being played open. The NBA, WNBA, college basketball and the NHL all changed; baseball keeps its own page for now. The pages are built from one set of parts, so a change to the look of the game page now reaches every sport at once.

entries.title: Touchdown picks stay out of player-prop parlays
entries.body: In football, an anytime-touchdown pick no longer rides in a three-leg or two-leg player-prop parlay. Touchdown scorers keep their own pairs, built as before. A moneyline, spread or total can't ride in a player-prop parlay in any league. On Friday's NFL board 28 touchdown legs and 4 moneylines were in those parlays, and those tickets are rebuilt from player props. It is also what had kept the one-sportsbook line quiet on some NFL parlays: a touchdown leg has no number to look up.

entries.title: Unders show their sportsbooks again
entries.body: When a sportsbook listed the same number on its main line and on its alternate ladder, we kept only the ladder's price, which is usually the over alone, so the under's price was lost. A parlay with an under said nothing about which one sportsbook has every leg, and a bet slip showed no current price for that under. Both read the main line's price now.

entries.title: A parlay says when a leg's number has moved
entries.body: A pick stays posted at the number it went up at. If the books move off that number before the game, a parlay with that leg now says it can't be placed as written, names the leg and gives the nearest number a book has. A new parlay does not take a leg like that, and Report Picks does not lead with one. The first board to count them had none.

entries.title: A price grade on NBA and NHL picks
entries.body: Each NBA and NHL player pick now shows whether its price is Green (the price needs no more than our number to break even), Yellow (up to 2 points more) or Red (more than that). It is on the game report, Report Picks and the Most Likely page. No pick is removed: since October the Red-priced picks have hit as often as the Green ones. The grade is about the price: among picks we gave 60% or better, the Green-priced ones made money and the Red-priced ones lost a little. Each card says how picks at its chance and grade have done on our record.

entries.title: Safe, Balanced or Pop on every parlay
entries.body: Every two-leg and three-leg parlay on a game report now says its class. Safe: every leg 64% or better and 40% together. Balanced: every leg 60% or better and 36% together. Pop: 25% together. Under that it is marked a long shot. Each card says why it is not the class above and names the one sportsbook that has every leg at its number, or says none does. The Record page splits each league's parlays by class.

entries.title: Two-leg parlays on every game report
entries.body: Every game report in every league now posts three two-leg player-prop parlays beside its three three-leg ones. Football and hockey keep their three touchdown or goal-scorer pairs. The two-leg tickets are built the same way: the report's own picks first, each at 40% or better by our numbers, and a posted ticket stays until one of its legs breaks. They had been basketball's alone, where they have hit more often than the three-leg ones.

entries.title: Football parlays and touchdown picks, tightened
entries.body: Football parlays no longer take a backup running back's yardage, a quarterback's rush-attempt under, a rushing over from a quarterback whose carries are mostly scrambles, or a pass catcher playing behind a new starting quarterback with too few passes to rate. A touchdown pair never puts two pass catchers from one team together. A touchdown pick between 40% and 45% now needs a plus-money price that pays for it to rank above Worth a look. Each of those picks stays on the board.

entries.title: College football props, held to their price
entries.body: A college football prop's chance is no longer shown higher than its own best price says. We checked every graded college prop since 26 September: the 617 we had rated above their price hit 55.1%, where we said 66.9% and the price said 57.1%. A game report's picks, the Most Likely tiers and the parlay legs now rank on the price's number for those picks, and each one says so. A price with only the over quoted no longer counts as the market agreeing with a pick.

entries.title: Two-leg parlays in basketball, and reads marked
entries.body: Every NBA, college basketball and WNBA game report now posts three two-leg player-prop parlays, where football posts its scorer pairs, built from the report's own picks. A pick on a market we can rank but not price yet, such as NFL rushing and receiving yards, is now marked as a read, not a bet: it still shows on the report and on Report Picks, says so, and isn't counted on the record.

entries.title: Three parlays and three scorer pairs a game
entries.body: Every game report now posts three three-leg player-prop parlays and three two-leg scorer pairs (touchdowns in football, goals in hockey; basketball has no scorer market). The report's own picks come first. A game short of them fills with our Most Likely picks and then its best props, and every leg that isn't one of the report's picks is named on its ticket. The two-leg player-prop parlays are retired.

entries.title: A game's parlays stay put
entries.body: A game's parlays no longer get swapped out every time a line moves. Once posted, a parlay stays up, at the books' current line, until one of its legs breaks: a player is ruled out, a book stops pricing the leg, or the parlay falls below its chance floor. Only that one is replaced.

entries.title: One set of parlays a game
entries.body: A finished game on Report Picks now lists only the parlays its report carried at kickoff. Games from before 16 November, when the site began keeping that set, had listed every version the board posted as lines moved, up to 42 a game; they now list none and say why. The Record never counted those versions.

entries.title: A live game's menu stays open
entries.body: The ⋯ menu on a live game's page could close by itself when the score updated just as you tapped it. It stays open now.

entries.title: Line Shopping in plain words
entries.body: The scanner's notes now say what each finding means without the jargon, and the glossary explains parlay, leg, push, sharp book, steam, arbitrage and middle.

entries.title: The likeliest tickets today, first
entries.body: Report Picks now opens on the three likeliest parlays of the games still to play, one per game: the legs, our chance and the price to take it at. Tap one to open its game.

entries.title: Our report parlays, followed live
entries.body: Every game report's parlays are now followed while the game is played: where each ticket stands, each leg's number so far and what it still needs. On the Live tab and on each live game's page, in every league.

entries.title: The game report's titles say their answers
entries.body: A folded section now carries its finding beside its title: who we think wins and the chance, the line, each club's unit edges, how many are listed and out, how many parlays, the breakout candidates and fades, the weather. In every league's report.

entries.title: Plain words in place of jargon
entries.body: "De-vigged" now reads "the books' fair price (their cut taken out)", a forecast comparison says which side has been closer to what happened, and the game page's replay panel says what its numbers mean.

entries.title: Parlay cards you can read at a glance
entries.body: Each ticket's chance is drawn large beside a bar filled to it, every leg wears its player's face, and the backups and caveats are set as small print. On the game report and on Report Picks.

entries.title: A game's day follows your clock
entries.body: A tip-off or first pitch is said whole in your time zone, its day with its clock. Outside the East the slate's date stood beside your clock, a day apart late at night.

entries.title: Report picks, split by where the report showed them
entries.body: The Record's game-report section now says how the card's picks, the matchup reads, the breakout candidates and the fades have each done, once two of them have results.

entries.title: A game's page wears its two clubs
entries.body: Before a game starts and after it ends, its page sits on both clubs' colours: the away club from the left, the home club from the right, like the live page. It works with the colour setting off and fades like every colour change.

entries.title: Cards say each thing once
entries.body: A parlay card gives its price caution once and a backup leg shared by every leg once. Today's Top Pick from another league says its number once, and a carried pick's note uses your clock.

entries.title: Last night's reports at a glance
entries.body: Report Picks opens with one card that sums the last slate: the reports' picks won and lost with units, each kind of parlay that hit, and how many calls were right, with a way to every game's picks and tickets. Free, for every league.

entries.title: Ask Qellys knows the rebuilt parlays
entries.body: Ask can say how the parlays built since 19 November have done, how last night's reports went, which leg of a ticket is not the report's own pick, and why a game has no parlays yet.

entries.title: Earlier parlay versions are said off the Record
entries.body: The Record counts one set of parlays a game: the set its report carried at the start. The list under each finished game still said every earlier version counted. It now says they do not, and Ask Qellys says the same.

entries.title: Every game with Most Likely picks can make its parlays
entries.body: A game report whose own picks are mostly ones a parlay never takes (touchdown scorers, tackles, game lines) had no three-leg parlay. Such a game now builds its tickets from our Most Likely picks for it, at 60% or better, on a ticket that clears 25%, each of those legs named on the ticket.

entries.title: Parlay legs keep our number until today's legs say otherwise
entries.body: The parlays' learned correction pulled every NFL leg all the way to the sportsbook's price, learned mostly from a retired source of legs that ran hot. It now learns only from legs built the way they are today, like its sister correction, so the report's own picks, which hit what they claim, keep their number until the record of today's legs says otherwise.

entries.title: A report's own picks always reach its parlays
entries.body: A game short of its three-leg parlays filled from its fourteen likeliest props, so on a game with many props priced the report's own picks under 60% were pushed out, and with them every ticket, since each takes two of the report's picks. They now enter first.

entries.title: A game with its props bought says why it has no parlay
entries.body: Sunday's NFL props were bought on Thursday, yet a game short of its two three-leg parlays still said its props were still to come. Once a game has its props priced, its report says the real reason, and that the books post more of its props as it nears.

entries.title: Two unders from one game share a parlay
entries.body: A game report's three-leg parlays may now pair two players' unders from the same game, which want the same quiet game: they were kept apart as a clash, which left reports whose best picks were unders with no parlay at all. Two teammates under on the same stat still stay apart, and an over that needs scoring never shares a ticket with an under that needs a quiet game.

entries.title: Sunday's NFL picks and parlays from Thursday
entries.body: The NFL board now prices each game's player props from three days before it, so Sunday's game reports carry their picks and parlays from Thursday, and Monday night's from Friday.

entries.title: Featured games: Lions games, Thursday nights and Monday nights
entries.body: NFL games the Lions play in, and those on Thursday and Monday nights, are featured: each report says so at its top with how games like it have done, ranks up to six picks instead of four, and the featured games keep their own record on Report Picks and the Record page, each kind and each game, with a chip that lists only them.

entries.title: The rebuilt parlays' own record
entries.body: Each league's parlay card on the Record page says how the tickets built since 19 November's rebuild have done, apart from the older ones.

entries.title: Parlays built from stronger legs, at honest chances
entries.body: A parlay's chance no longer counts a link between its legs that our record says does not hold, so each game's tickets lead with its strongest picks. A game short of tickets fills with its report's own picks first and other props only at 60% or better, and markets benched for losing money are left out of parlays.

entries.title: Three-leg parlays on the last few short games
entries.body: A game with three or more props at 50% or better but no two three-leg parlays can now make them as longer tickets, down to 12.5% by our numbers, each saying how long it is on its card.

entries.title: Every game report has its parlays section
entries.body: A game whose player props have not been priced yet now says so where its parlays will be, and when they come: an NFL Sunday game's props are bought the day before it. A game whose props all sit between 50% and 60% now gets its two three-leg parlays from them.

entries.title: Two three-leg parlays on more games
entries.body: A game with too few props at 60% or better to make two three-leg parlays now fills them with props down to 50%, each such leg named on its card.

entries.title: A lighter first visit
entries.body: The code the Alerts page alone uses now loads when that page opens, not on every first visit, so the site starts with less to download.

entries.title: College basketball players' real positions
entries.body: College basketball rosters now come from each school's published roster, so players show as guards, forwards and centers, with numbers and heights, on the Rosters page, in the player search and on player pages, instead of a box score's starter mark.

entries.title: The Most Likely record, said once
entries.body: The Record page showed the Most Likely record four times under three different counts. It is the top tile now; the sections below it keep what only they say: each tier, how often the picks hit against what we said, and each half's size and return.

entries.title: The parlay record counts one set a game
entries.body: The Record page's game parlays now count the tickets each game report carried when its game started, and no version the board posted and replaced before then. The page says how many others it left out.

entries.title: Last season's final standings stay up through the offseason
entries.body: A league's standings page in its offseason still says when the next season opens, and now shows the season that finished under it: the final table, the postseason as it was played, labelled final.

entries.title: Three-leg parlays back on every game report
entries.body: Every game report shows two or three three-leg parlays again, built from the report's own picks first. Where the picks are too few, the game's other priced props fill in, and each such ticket says which legs are not the report's picks, and when it is a longer shot than we usually build.

entries.title: Every league in the strategy lab, and hockey on the prediction desk
entries.body: The Toolbox's strategy lab can now test a rule on college basketball and the WNBA too, with the two college sports named. The prediction-market desk puts our chance beside Kalshi's NHL games and files hockey trades under the NHL. The race pages write their game counts with commas, and the Alerts page says once where your watched players and teams show up.

entries.title: Hockey's opening week counted in this season
entries.body: The NHL season opened on 29 September this year, and its first eight games had been filed under last season, so fifteen clubs' pages, the playoff race and those players' season lines were a game short. Every hockey game now counts in the season it belongs to, and a goalie's starts are counted in every stored game.

entries.title: A fighter's page found, and the injury report counted fairly
entries.body: Searching from the UFC tab now finds fighters and opens their page, and a fighter's link reloads to the fighter. A college quarterback's chart names the right opponent, a hockey goalie's starts are counted, and a report's injury record counts the players it listed, with the regulars it missed said beside it.

entries.title: A stadium said once, and the Streak names its league
entries.body: A game page now says a stadium's roof and surface once each, and an exchange line at the same price on Polymarket and Kalshi shows once, naming both. The Streak names the league of each question when a night mixes leagues, and a Record page's profit calendar opens on the book that has settled days.

entries.title: College ranks out of Division I, and a playoff week says its round
entries.body: A college team page now ranks a school among Division I, not every school on file. Charts name a split season the way the pages do (2025–26), a team page says its record once, an NFL player’s last ten names a playoff game by its round, and a player page shows an injury tag even when opened first.

entries.title: Seasons read as their leagues say them, and each number once
entries.body: A basketball or hockey team page now says 2026–27, as the player page does. The team page's last games show once, a player page's shot chart no longer repeats the previous game's card, and the Record page names which book each settled pick is from, writes headline picks as bets (“BOS@ORL over 222.5”) and says the Edge picks' calibration is theirs.

entries.title: Under pressure for basketball: reliability, comeback and choke
entries.body: Those three need to know who the market favored, and basketball games were stored without a line. They now use the last price our board saw before each game, so they fill in through this season as teams play enough games.

entries.title: College ranks are out of Division I
entries.body: A college game’s matchup scan ranked schools out of 407, counting small schools that played a few Division I teams, so every school looked lower than it is. Ranks are now out of Division I’s 365, and a small school still shows its numbers.

entries.title: Game pages say what they have, once
entries.body: Before a game’s props are priced, its page now says so plainly instead of saying the same nothing twice. The Under pressure table shows only the numbers that exist for that league, without empty columns.

entries.title: The chat’s Big plays tab keeps your place
entries.body: A reaction on any play, or the game’s own refresh every few seconds, sent the Big plays tab back to the top and a play’s thread back to its end. Counts now change on their own card, and you stay where you were.

entries.title: The game chat holds still, and reactions show on a phone
entries.body: The chat redrew its scoreboard, buttons and tabs every three seconds, so taps could miss. Now it only changes what changed. On a phone each message has a small face to tap for reactions and Reply. Message times keep up, sending keeps your keyboard open, and a reaction that doesn’t go through says so.

entries.title: Team pages load in seconds, not half a minute
entries.body: A team page could take up to half a minute the first time it opened. It now reads only that team’s games, so it opens in a few seconds.

entries.title: A slow team page no longer says the team doesn’t exist
entries.body: When a team page took too long to load, it could say no team matched. Now it says the page couldn’t load and to try again.

entries.title: Benched parlays are labeled benched
entries.body: When a league’s parlays are benched for losing, the report posts none. How our reports did listed every benched version as the report’s own anyway. Now they sit apart, marked never posted.

entries.title: No parlays once a hockey game starts
entries.body: Hockey’s picks did not carry their game’s start time, so parlays kept being built after the puck dropped. They now stop at the start, and so do the game’s Edge picks, as in basketball.

entries.title: No pick says it’s certain
entries.body: A Most Likely pick went up at 100% because every one of the player’s recent games went its way. A chance that high now keeps a pick off the board: no bet is certain.

entries.title: Hockey’s playoff race counts each game once
entries.body: The race could replay games already won and lost, because the schedule it read was a day old. A game from before today is never simulated again.

entries.title: Each team’s own game count
entries.body: A game page’s matchup scan could say 9 games at the top and 10 below when one team had a bye. It gives each team’s count now, and says the season split once.

entries.title: Per-game numbers after Monday night
entries.body: Rushing yards and sacks allowed a game read low for the Monday night teams until that game’s plays came in. Each now divides by the games it has.

entries.title: College football counts each game once
entries.body: Western Michigan read 9-3 with one game at Buffalo counted twice. A game filed under two names for one team counts once now, and the college standings ask for the right table.

entries.title: Team pages open faster in every league
entries.body: NFL, hockey and NBA team pages still read far more than their own team. They read only the team’s own games and roster now.

entries.title: Team pages open faster
entries.body: A college basketball team’s page could take half a minute to open, reading every season’s box scores to find one team’s. It reads that team’s own games now.

entries.title: The record’s curve ends on its last day
entries.body: A handful of Week 1 football bets kept their week’s label and were drawn after November on the Record page’s curve. They sit in their own week now, and the curve’s dates read as days.

entries.title: Headlines are news, not offers
entries.body: Each league’s headlines no longer carry sportsbook sign-up offers or a publisher’s every-sport betting roundup. The injuries page uses each league’s own words for who is out, and says each team’s count once, and the UFC card counts every bout.

entries.title: College rankings are this week’s poll
entries.body: The tournament race showed some schools with last week’s poll rank beside others with this week’s, so two schools could share a number while others were missing. It reads the current AP Top 25 now and says so.

entries.title: Dates, signs and labels put right
entries.body: Injury return dates read as days, a hockey player’s plus-minus carries its sign, the UFC record’s return is labelled against what was staked, and a board whose picks are for members says so instead of calling the slate empty.

entries.title: Hockey goalies measured on every chance they faced
entries.body: A goalie’s goals saved above expected now count missed shots, as the expected-goals model is built on them, so tonight’s starters no longer all read far below expected. Shooters’ goals, points and assists against a confirmed starter had been priced up to a fifth too likely; those chances come down. Hockey’s game lines do not move.

entries.title: Futures say when they are for members
entries.body: The Futures page told visitors there was no season to project when the board was there and kept for members; it now says so. A college basketball team’s page is headed by the school’s name, and a team search that finds nothing gives an example from its own league.

entries.title: Small words put right across the site
entries.body: The Streak counts from zero and locks each pick when its own game starts; hockey says puck drop; the plans page names a school without “the” and says what its closing-line number measures; the Record page calls college basketball NCAAB everywhere and stops repeating a ribbon and a note; Zeno’s page names a past week by its dates.

entries.title: Every league named where the leagues are listed
entries.body: The About page, the plans and the search description listed six or seven leagues; they now name all eight, with About cards for the NHL and college basketball, and My Bets can file a bet under NHL or NCAAB. My Bets also says where your log is kept by whether you are signed in, and the Status page says what the UFC card holds.

entries.title: Parlay legs by market add up
entries.body: On the Record page, each league’s game parlay card counted its legs once in the headline but every ticket a leg rode in the by-market rows, so a market could show more legs than the whole card. The market rows now count each bet once and add up to the headline.

entries.title: Recent team changes show real moves only
entries.body: The rosters page could list a player moving to a team and straight back when the players feed had the wrong club for a few days. A move that is taken back now drops off; real moves, including a player who moved twice, still show.

entries.title: College football standings count each game once
entries.body: The college football standings counted some games two or three times, so records like Utah 19-0 showed in November. Each game now counts once in the table, the offense and defense rankings, the pressure numbers and the season simulation.

entries.title: The UFC tab’s numbers are right for everyone
entries.body: The UFC tab’s Picks count showed “[object Object]” to visitors, and its modeled and waiting counts read 0 on a full card. Both are right now, a locked pass list says it is for members instead of “Nothing to pass on”, and the record is said once.

entries.title: Report Picks, Edge and quiet boards say it once and say it right
entries.body: The locked Report Picks page no longer repeats what it is four times. The Edge page with nothing on shows a dash for the average edge instead of a green “+0.0%”, and no “0 props · 0 game bets — all journaled”. A board waiting on props no longer says “MLB” on other leagues, and a day with no games says so.

entries.title: College basketball teams go by their school
entries.body: College basketball pages named teams by mascot (“Cougars 85”) while college football and our reports named the school. They now say the school (“Houston 85”), with the mascot over it on the live scoreboards, and the Pick of the Day says which Wildcats it means.

entries.title: College and WNBA pace in their own 40-minute game
entries.body: Pace on a college or WNBA game page read as possessions per 48 minutes, a game length neither league plays. The tale of the tape, the game report and its fact check now say possessions per 40 minutes there (the NBA stays per 48). Only the words and the numbers shown changed; our reads are the same.

entries.title: A finished game’s page says each thing once
entries.body: The final score no longer shows twice (the page’s header, then the report card under it): the card now heads itself “How our report did”. The locked report preview names the report once and, on a finished game, says it was written before the game rather than from tonight’s board. And a finished game no longer says books haven’t posted prop prices yet.

entries.title: Every finished game gets its final score
entries.body: A few late games never got their final on file (the Nuggets at Phoenix and the Lakers at Golden State on 30 October, the Bruins at Anaheim on 16 October, and some hockey games with no row at all), so a team page’s record could be a game behind its standings. Each night now reads again any recent day where a game has no final, and hockey also checks each club’s own schedule for a finished game we do not have.

entries.title: A search names each team once, with bigger team chips
entries.body: Searching a team’s name showed it twice: as a team chip and again as a “player” (the feeds list a club’s defence under the club’s own name). It is the team chip alone now, and the chips are bigger. On a player’s page the season card carries the games played and the other counts (targets, attempts) as small pills, where the big season box under the chart used to repeat them.

entries.title: Quarterback completions and NBA points go on the bench
entries.body: Two Edge markets lost all season: the NFL’s quarterback completions (44-53, −11.9 units) and the NBA’s points (63-71, −10.2 units). Their picks still post and are graded, but they carry no stake, stay out of the staked record and say “Tracked · no stake” on the card. Each comes back to stakes by itself once 60 picks graded since the bench make money at flat stakes. The Record page lists the markets on the bench and where each stands.

entries.title: A game’s parlays lead with its two strongest picks
entries.body: The report picks were hitting and the three-leg parlays built from them were not: three picks have to all hit, and a night’s picks at 4 of 5 still lose every ticket holding the one miss. Each game now leads with its two strongest picks as a two-leg parlay, and a three-leg parlay is made only when our own numbers give it 30% or better. The two-leg parlays have their own record on the Record page, and the parlay legs now learn market by market, so a market whose legs hit less than we said gets marked down.

entries.title: A team’s page stops counting games with no betting line
entries.body: A game with no line on file read “0 covered” or “0 missed” on a team’s schedule, and the record against the spread beside it was just the win-loss record. Those games now say nothing about the spread, and the tile shows only a real record. On basketball pages the box score’s starter mark (S or B) is no longer printed as a position: rosters read Starters and Bench, and the leaders are most points, rebounds and assists. An injury says its word once (“Concussion”, not twice) with the return day as a day.

entries.title: The Record page says each thing once
entries.body: The week’s card printed codes for markets (“fg3m”, “pts reb”, “stl”) and a book name no page uses; it now says 3-Pointers Made, Pts+Reb and Steals, and names its books as their sections do. A league’s record listed its report picks and tickets twice, in flat lists and again game by game; the flat lists now give way to one line that links to each game’s. A one-row “By kind” that repeated the tile above it is gone.

entries.title: A player’s page says each thing once
entries.body: A player’s page said who the player is three times, the season’s totals twice and the last game’s line seven times. The header now holds the club’s link and Copy link; the chart no longer repeats the name card or the score of the game shown above it; the split rows no longer list one game twice; the markets card lost its second header and its extra doors to the charts and game log. A quarterback no longer gets Receiving Yards chips off one fluke catch.

entries.title: NFL road games read “@”, not “vs”
entries.body: Every NFL game in a player’s By market list was labelled a home game: a Week 10 game at the Jets read “vs NYJ”. The weekly stats never say where a game was played, so the schedule now does. This season is corrected at the next results pull and earlier seasons over the next few nights.

entries.title: Season projections and playoff brackets follow the night’s results
entries.body: Every feed on the site was timed: boards, standings, injuries and news were minutes old and live scores seconds old. One was behind. The season projections and the NBA’s and NHL’s playoff brackets were rebuilt once a day, so after a night’s games they could read up to a day behind the standings beside them. A league whose results have changed is now rebuilt within about 45 minutes. And a standings page waiting on a season says when the league opens (“It opens in late March 2027”) instead of the first day of its calendar window.

entries.title: A team’s page wears its colours, and colour changes fade
entries.body: Open any team’s page and the whole screen sits on that club’s two colours, as a player’s page does, whether or not you wear a team’s colours yourself; leave it and the screen is yours again. Every change of the screen’s colours now fades smoothly instead of snapping: your colours to a club’s and back, one page’s club to the next, into and out of a game. The button on a team’s page now reads “Wear these everywhere”.

entries.title: A game that ends after the board moves on is still fact-checked
entries.body: A report was fact-checked only while its game was still on the board, and college football’s board moves to its next slate at midnight Eastern, with Saturday’s late games still being played. A game that finishes after that, or whose box score arrives late in any league, is now graded and kept from the report written before its start, with its picks and parlays.

entries.title: The welcome page shows the game report and everything else
entries.body: The first screen now shows what a game report holds, from who we think wins to the parlays made of its picks and how it grades itself after the final, with the reports’ own record and the newest game they fact-checked, right or wrong. Under it, a tile for every other feature says whether it is free or for members, and the Features page now leads with the game reports.

entries.title: A game with fewer than four parlays says why
entries.body: A game’s parlays are made only of its report’s own picks, so a report whose picks fit together into one to three tickets posts just those. The game page and Report Picks now say why under them, instead of only when a game has none.

entries.title: A parlay that takes a team to win is graded on the game
entries.body: Some of the first week’s three-leg parlays took a team to win beside two player props. That leg had nothing of its own to grade from, so it was voided, and a ticket whose team lost could read won on its props (Monday night’s Ravens ticket did). It is now graded on the game’s final score, and every ticket graded the old way is put right on the next nightly check. Any parlay leg with nothing of its own to grade from now grades from the same bet in our other pick lists, or off the box score like any other pick, so the parlays still waiting days after their game settle too, and none is voided on a player who played.

entries.title: Each game’s parlays are made of its report’s own picks
entries.body: A game’s three-leg parlays were built from every prop we priced at 60% or better, and more than half their legs were never one of the report’s picks: Monday’s NBA picks hit 41 of 62 while the parlays went 4 of 30, sunk mostly by legs the report never picked. Now each game’s parlays are built only from the picks its report shows, under the same rules, and a game whose picks make fewer than four says why. Parlays that sat “waiting on the box score” for days because a leg had nothing to grade from now settle, that leg voided the way a book voids it.

entries.title: The tab bar stays at the bottom of the screen as you scroll
entries.body: On an iPhone the app could go on drawing itself above a keyboard that had already gone (another app’s, beside it in Split View, counts), so the tab bar, the live pill and the page’s light stood halfway up the screen and slid with the page. The installed app now measures how far the screen stands from where those are pinned and moves them back by exactly that, every frame, letting go the moment the phone puts things right or one of the app’s own boxes takes the keyboard. When nothing is wrong, nothing moves.

entries.title: College quarterbacks get a passing chart
entries.body: Every college throw and sack is now charted: each completion drawn to where the play ended, the misses, picks and sacks marked, a season shaded by how far the completions went, and splits by down and by receiver. The play file doesn’t record how far the ball travelled or to which side, so the chart says so. A college receiver’s season is drawn the same way, so a busy one’s targets no longer pile into one shape.

entries.title: Every fighter’s page has a photo, the facts and the fights
entries.body: A fighter who was not on the coming card had a page with a record and no photo, height, reach or fight history. Every fighter we keep is now read, and a searched fighter shows a face like every league’s players.

entries.title: The 2026 baseball season fills its box scores by itself
entries.body: Each night now reads more of the 2026 season’s box scores until every MLB player’s page carries the whole line, newest games first.

entries.title: Ask knows a baseball player’s whole line
entries.body: Ask can now answer with RBIs, runs, walks, stolen bases and a pitcher’s earned runs, hits and walks allowed: who leads the league, and how often a player has cleared a number.

entries.title: No more charts of zeros on a player’s market card
entries.body: A football player’s market chips are now the roles they play: a quarterback is no longer offered receiving yards, receptions and targets, ten games of zeros.

entries.title: The last game’s card shows what the player did
entries.body: A player’s last-game card no longer shows a row of zeros for a game they spent another way: a quarterback who only ran that week shows the runs.

entries.title: Baseball splits as totals, and a hitter’s against lefties and righties
entries.body: An MLB player’s splits now add the games up, the way a box score is read, with the averages beside them, and a hitter’s Splits menu shows how they hit against left-handed and right-handed starters.

entries.title: Every fighter’s page has a face and the facts
entries.body: A fighter whose fights we have not tracked yet now has a face, height, reach and stance on their page too, from what was kept when their profile was drafted.

entries.title: The player page draws the charts, and its tables’ first column is solid
entries.body: A player’s page draws their charts on the Overview again, under the last game: the route chart, the throws, the carries, the spray chart, the pitches, the shots or the shot map, for the market you came for. And the game column that stays put while a table scrolls no longer lets the numbers behind it show through.

entries.title: The watch card names the bets a move touches
entries.body: When a player moves on the injury report after a game’s report was written, the card at the top now says which of that report’s picks and parlay legs name them, with the parlay’s backup leg, and to wait for the next update before betting it.

entries.title: MLB player pages carry the whole box-score line
entries.body: An MLB player’s page and game log now show the full line a box score prints: AB, R, H, 2B, 3B, HR, RBI, BB, SO, SB and total bases with AVG, OBP, SLG and OPS for a hitter, and innings, hits, runs, earned runs, walks, strikeouts, homers, pitches and the decision with ERA and WHIP for a pitcher. The game log’s rates read as the season through each game, and a hitter’s page leads with AVG, HR, RBI and OPS, a pitcher’s with ERA, strikeouts, WHIP and innings, each ranked in the league.

entries.title: Every fighter has a full page
entries.body: Searching a fighter on the UFC tab opens their own page, like every other league’s player page: the record, nickname, height, reach and age up top, then the career rates and the next fight, every tracked fight with how it ended and both fighters’ numbers, striking and grappling stats, a bio and the news.

entries.title: NFL three-leg parlays go on paper
entries.body: Our NFL three-leg parlays have hit 30 of 175 (17%), so they are no longer posted. Each game’s are still built and graded on the record, and they come back on their own once fifty graded from today hit 25%. Any league whose three-leg parlays fall under 25% goes on paper the same way. The touchdown pairs are unchanged.

entries.title: A pick opens the player’s page
entries.body: Tapping a player’s pick on Most Likely, the Edge board or anywhere else a pick is listed now opens that player’s page, with the pick you tapped at the top: the line and price, the chance, the case for it and why it’s likely, with its chart. The rest of that market’s numbers are further down the same page. Game bets and UFC fights still open their own page.

entries.title: Game reports keep watch on injuries and the news
entries.body: Every five minutes, each upcoming game’s report checks the injury report and the news. A player whose status moves (questionable to out, cleared to play) and the latest headlines about either team show on the game’s page as soon as we see them, over the report, until kickoff. The next report written folds them into its own text. Every league with game reports, not just the NFL.

entries.title: A goal flashes on the live hockey score
entries.body: Like the touchdown flash on football: when a side scores while you’re watching the game’s page, its score pulses gold with GOAL over it for a few seconds. Not on opening the page, and not for a shootout.

entries.title: College basketball’s usage chart says 2026–27
entries.body: The usage chart on a college basketball player’s page called the season “2026”; it now reads “2026–27”, like the rest of the page and the NBA’s.

entries.title: Hockey’s open bets go live with the game, and hockey joins the streak
entries.body: An open hockey bet on the Live tab could still read “upcoming” after the puck dropped: it now follows the live scoreboard like football and basketball. The free streak game now draws its daily questions from hockey’s board too.

entries.title: A game with no stats says so on the player page
entries.body: A game a player recorded nothing in read “The box score isn’t in yet” for weeks afterwards. It now reads “No stats recorded” once the box score has had its days, and a player with no games played this season shows the last season they did play, said as such.

entries.title: The Lab replays hockey, and Ask knows hockey
entries.body: The Lab’s weekly replay now grades hockey’s shots, points, goals, assists, blocks, anytime goal and saves the way it grades the other leagues. Ask Qellys reads hockey’s live scoreboard and knows a hockey team named in words (“Oilers at Flames”).

entries.title: Hockey has its own address and is on every league list
entries.body: qellysbook.com/nhl now opens the NHL board, a shared hockey player, game or pick opens the right page, “Tonight, every league” includes hockey’s slate, swiping between leagues stops on it, and Settings → Leagues in the nav lists it. Hockey players also get the “History vs a team” box.

entries.title: Every college game is named on How our reports did
entries.body: A college game whose report called no winner was listed by its codes (“espn:2145 63 at DEN 101”). It now reads with the schools’ names (“UC Col Springs 63 at Denver 101”).

entries.title: An All-Star Game is no player’s form
entries.body: Every WNBA All-Star Game since 2023, the NBA’s All-Star games and preseason exhibitions against national teams were stored as games of the season, so they counted in a player’s averages, recent form and hit rates. The nightly now keeps a game only when both sides are the league’s own clubs, in the NBA and the WNBA, and the ones already stored are being removed.

entries.title: Playoff games by their round
entries.body: A player’s page and Game Log called an NFL playoff game “Week 20”, the number the league’s files give it. They now say Wild Card, Divisional, Conference title game or Super Bowl (WC, DIV, CONF and SB in the log).

entries.title: WNBA pages head with minutes, not an empty FG%
entries.body: The WNBA box scores we keep have no shots, so every WNBA player’s page ended its four headline numbers with “FG% —”. A headline number with nothing behind it now gives way to minutes a game, ranked like the rest.

entries.title: A new league clears the player’s address
entries.body: Tapping another league on a player’s page showed that league’s list but kept the player’s address, so a reload or a shared link opened the old name in the new league. The address now goes back to the list.

entries.title: A player’s page is never a near name’s
entries.body: College basketball’s page for Cooper Flagg, who is in the NBA now, showed TJ Cope’s numbers because “Cope” is close to “Cooper”. A page, a game log or a matchup history now takes a near name only when the whole name is a misspelling, and a page for a name the league has nobody by says so instead of “This page could not load”.

entries.title: Solid cards for more contrast
entries.body: On a phone set to reduce transparency or increase contrast, the cards on a player’s page are solid again over the club’s colours instead of dark glass.

entries.title: This feed and the privacy page read the same for every player
entries.body: The older entries on this page called a player “he” and “his” (“his share of his team’s carries”); they say “they” and “their” now, except where they name a player. The privacy policy said a fantasy alert carries a starter’s “his name and his designation”; it now says the player’s name and designation.

entries.title: A player’s page in the club’s colours
entries.body: A player’s page now sits on the club’s two colours the way a live game’s page sits on its clubs’: the top bar and the page are one picture, the name lies on the colours at night, and the cards are dark glass over them. White, silver and grey are treated as trim, so the Maple Leafs and Duke are blue on deeper blue. While the page is open the search steps aside behind “Back to the search”.

entries.title: The search box speaks each league
entries.body: The Players search box suggested “Amon-Ra, Rams” on every league’s tab. It now gives an example from the league you are searching: “Tatum, Celtics” on the NBA, “McDavid, Oilers” on the NHL, and a fighter on UFC.

entries.title: A player page with no numbers says why
entries.body: A punter’s or a lineman’s page opened on an empty Overview. It now leads with the reason there are no numbers, the same line its Stats and Game Log menus show, and a fantasy team defense says what it is.

entries.title: The player card’s chart follows an under pick
entries.body: The market card on a player’s page coloured every game by whether it went over the line, whatever the pick was, so an under’s winning games showed red and the count read “cleared”. The games the pick won are green now and the count names the side (“4/8 under 26.5”). On a computer the chart keeps its height instead of growing across the whole card.

entries.title: The sim lab follows an under pick
entries.body: The “Run tonight ×2,000” lab under a pick shaded and counted the over even when the pick was an under, so a 62% under read “the model says 38%”. It now shades and counts the side the pick wins on, and shows its curve faintly before the first run.

entries.title: The board’s notes read the same for every player
entries.body: The notes the board writes onto the cards and the game reports no longer call players “he” or “his”, and the NBA’s notes are the WNBA’s too: “Minutes up 20% over the last five”, “In the 6 games Bam Adebayo missed, this player took 17% of MIA’s points”, “Not in BOS’s likely starting five tonight”, “Jaylen Brown is now out (listed questionable before)”. The MLB, NHL, UFC, college, fantasy and slip-check notes read the same way.

entries.title: The rest of the site reads the same for every player
entries.body: The last pages that called players “he” or “his” no longer do: the Lab cards on a pick (“How the books set the line”, “The role, watched for a change”), the Most Likely page (“We have the player at 58.2 receiving yards”), the fantasy draft room (“Will they last?”) and the week’s start-or-sit call, which now says START or SIT.

entries.title: The charts read the same for every player
entries.body: The carry, route, passing, hit, pitch, shot, save, role, kicker and fight charts no longer call players “he” or “his”: a WNBA player’s shot chart said “where he shoots”. They read “Where the shots come from”, “Season average”, “Last 6 fights”, and a fight’s numbers name the fighter.

entries.title: NFL photos for every Jr., Sr. and II
entries.body: A third of the NFL players whose names end in Jr., Sr., II, III or IV had no photo on the rosters and their pages, because the photo list spells their names without the suffix. A photo is now found by the league’s own player id first, then by the name, then by ESPN’s id.

entries.title: A search lists names, and a name opens the player’s page
entries.body: The Players search now answers with each player’s face and name, and lists tonight’s players the same way before anything is typed. Tapping a name opens that player’s page, with tonight’s markets and their chart on it. The market card there no longer opens a separate pick page: it has Bet it and Ask on it instead. Back returns to the search with the words still in the box. A player whose roster spells the name with “Jr.” or “Sr.” is one row, not two.

entries.title: Every player page is the right player
entries.body: A name on a roster only ever opens that player now: before, Anthony Richardson Sr.’s page showed Anthony Gould’s, and Nolan Smith Jr.’s was empty because box scores drop the “Jr.” A page with nothing to show says why: a fantasy team defense, a player whose games recorded no stats, or a college school whose games we don’t cover.

entries.title: A player with no games never shows someone else’s
entries.body: A player with no games on file, like a punter, could open the page of the nearest name we did have: JK Scott’s showed Nick Scott’s tackles. A near name now stands in only when it is the same player: the same name written another way, a typo, or a near name on the same club.

entries.title: Hockey and basketball pages show more of the box score
