entries.body: A skater who hasn’t scored yet this season no longer has an empty page and game log: the page chose its stats by the goals column alone. Hockey pages now show plus-minus and penalty minutes, and basketball pages show three-point and free-throw percentages beside the makes.

entries.title: Kickers’ and defenders’ pages have their numbers
entries.body: A kicker’s page leads with field goals made, field goal percentage, the longest and kicking points, each with its place in the league, and the Stats and Game Log tabs show every game’s field goals, extra points and points. A defender’s page leads with tackles, sacks, interceptions and passes defended, with solo tackles, tackles for loss, quarterback hits, forced fumbles and touchdowns in the tabs. College kickers have their field goals too. A punter’s page now says our stats feed doesn’t include punting, and a lineman’s that box scores keep no numbers for linemen, instead of looking empty.

entries.title: Every page reads the same for every player
entries.body: The parlay notes, the matchup charts, the teammate notes, the slip grader, Start A or B, the fantasy week and the alerts no longer call players “he” or “his”: “If that player sits”, “The player’s targets”, “Start Josh Allen: Allen outscores Patrick Mahomes 62% of the time”.

entries.title: The NBA’s and the NHL’s playoff races
entries.body: The Playoff race page now draws the NBA’s and the NHL’s playoffs as brackets: who is in if the season ended today and who plays whom, the NBA’s play-in for the 7 and 8 seeds and the NHL’s two wild cards a conference, the clubs just outside and how far back they are, and the tables that decide it. Members see every club’s chance to make the playoffs, win its conference and win the title, from the same seasons the Futures page plays, which now follow each league’s own format. The NBA’s page keeps its Cup one tap away, and the NHL’s Futures and Playoff race pages are open.

entries.title: Season outlooks count the games already played
entries.body: The Futures page’s season simulation now starts every league from its real standings. Since August it had started each team at 0-0 and played out only the games left, so every playoff, division and title chance ignored the results so far. Hockey’s table reads W-L-OT, with an overtime or shootout loss worth a point, and a playoff game no longer counts in the regular season.

entries.title: The prop cards' notes read the same for every player
entries.body: The scouting warnings and matchup notes on every prop card no longer call players “he” or “his”: “an over while the player’s role has been shrinking”, “58% of the targets are short throws”, “If that player sits, our projection moves +18% catches”.

entries.title: Football's parlay legs learn their own correction
entries.body: The NFL’s three-leg parlay legs claimed 68% and hit 55%, and the books’ prices on them said 68% too, so pulling them toward the books could not fix them. Every league’s legs now also learn a direct correction from their own results, kept only when it scores the newest legs better, and only from legs built the way they are built today. Football’s legs are recalibrated by this week’s games.

entries.title: Your teams on the bracket
entries.body: Every team you follow is lit with a star wherever a playoff bracket draws it, and the NFL’s Playoff race page opens with where each of your teams stands: its seed if the season ended today, or how far back of the 7 seed, and for members its chance to make the playoffs.

entries.title: The game reports read the same for every player
entries.body: The reports, their after-game checks and the game parlays no longer call players “he” or “his”: “the last 6 games”, “Right: played — 22 points”, “the touchdown matchup backs it”. The practice line now reads “last practice of the week: limited”.

entries.title: One bracket for every playoff
entries.body: The NBA Cup’s knockout rounds and the College Football Playoff now draw as the same bracket as the NFL’s race: lines joining each game to the next, the East and West facing each other across the Cup final, college’s first-round games beside the quarterfinal their winners play. Each game shows the seeds, the score once played with the winner highlighted, the night and the site, and our line while it is still to play.

entries.title: Ask Qellys reads every game report
entries.body: Ask can now open any game’s report by team: who we think wins and why, the angles, the red zone, how the game should go, and the report’s own picks and parlays. Ask about a finished game and it says how the report did — the call, the reads, the injury report — and how each pick and each parlay leg finished. It also knows how our reports have done over the season, the report picks’ and game parlays’ records, and every playoff race: the seeds, who is just outside, each team’s chances and the games that swing it.

entries.title: The playoff race is drawn as a bracket
entries.body: The NFL’s and college football’s playoff races now show the field as a bracket instead of seed lists: every club with its logo, seed, record and why it is in, the first round’s games paired the way the playoffs pair them, and lines joining each game to the next. The later rounds say who meets whom. On a computer the AFC and NFC face each other across the Super Bowl; on a phone each swipes through its rounds. The clubs just outside are listed under it with how far back they are.

entries.title: Every finished game marks its picks and parlays
entries.body: On How our reports did, every finished game now shows a check or an X for each of its report’s picks and for each parlay and pair the report carried at the start, with how many hit (and how the board’s earlier versions of them did). Tap it to see every pick by name with the number it finished with, and every parlay with each of its legs marked. Settled picks show to everyone; members also see the ones still waiting on the box score. The list now loads 20 games at a time.

entries.title: Your team’s colours on the whole site
entries.body: Settings → Team colours now has three choices: off, the bar, or the whole site. On the whole site, every page sits on your team’s two colours the way a live game’s page sits on its two teams’, from the top of the screen down into the page, with the top bar painted the same so there is no line between them. Pick whose colours under it, or tap Wear these colours on any team’s page. The colours are darkened just enough for white words to read on them, and the light theme wears them as a soft tint.

entries.title: The game log wears the team’s colours
entries.body: A player’s game log now opens on a header in the team’s colours with the player’s photo, on the team’s colour like a live game’s page. Every game shows the other team’s logo, and each result is a green or red pill. The player page’s Game Log and Recent games get the logos and pills too.

entries.title: The whole site wears its own light
entries.body: Every page now sits on a soft gold glow that rises from the top of the screen and fades into the page, with a faint amber warmth in the far corner, in both the dark and the light theme. A player’s page and a team’s page glow in that club’s colour instead, and a team’s page opens on a band in its colours like a player’s does. The game and live pages keep their two-team colours.

entries.title: Parlay legs learn their own correction, league by league
entries.body: Our parlay legs had been hitting less often than the chance we gave them, most of all in the NFL. Each league now learns from its own graded legs how far to move each leg’s chance toward the sportsbook’s, and uses it only when it would also have called the newest legs better. What moved on the board: a leg’s chance on the game parlays and touchdown pairs, and with it which legs clear the 60% bar, once a league has 60 graded legs.

entries.title: The two-leg parlays’ record is retired
entries.body: The Record page no longer shows the retired two-leg parlays or the old parlay screen. The parlays it shows are each game report’s, under The Game Report Picks and Parlays. Every ticket the two retired products made is still kept in our record.

entries.title: A finished game says if its report was right
entries.body: A finished game’s page now opens on one verdict in color: the report got the game mostly right, half right or mostly wrong, from its pick to win and its reads. Under it, a row for each thing the report said and each kind of bet, green where it held and red where it missed: the pick to win, the reads by kind, our picks, the 3-leg parlays and touchdown pairs, the injury report, the touchdown chances, our ratings and the simulation, and the lines. Then what it got right and what it got wrong, by name. When a game’s page no longer holds its picks, they come from our record, each listed with how it went. The grades read in plainer words, and a single touchdown against a small average no longer tops the best calls.

entries.title: Ohio State is Ohio State again
entries.body: ESPN’s list of college teams gives “OSU” to two schools, Ohio State and Ohio State Newark, and our college pages kept the second: Ohio State’s games would have shown the Newark Titans’ name and colours, its older games stayed filed under an ESPN number, and its roster was missing from the roster page. When two schools share an abbreviation now, the major program keeps it. Ohio State’s history is filed under OSU again on the next college build, and its roster returns with the next roster build. Re-filing it briefly dropped a few box-score lines that the play-by-play file credits to the other side (Jeremiah Smith’s 11 catches against NU); the box score’s line now wins in that case, and it is restored on the next settle.

entries.title: Player search is fast in every league
entries.body: Searching an NHL, MLB or college basketball player could take 15 to 25 seconds: to count a player’s games, the search read every game line the player had ever logged. It now counts them from its index of players, answers from the list of names it has while a newer one is built in the background, and lists a college player at their school, not at a number like “espn:194”. A player’s page also no longer takes a namesake’s school and position for its header when the player’s own roster is missing, nor the other side’s school from a copy of a game filed with the two teams swapped.

entries.title: Parlay legs claim what they hit
entries.body: Football’s game parlay legs were hitting about half the time against the two in three we gave them. Our single picks at those chances hit what they said; the parlays were also taking props whose number sat further above the book’s than our own picks allow, and keeping the higher of two chances for the same bet. A parlay now takes a prop only when our pick rules stand behind its number, the same bet’s Most Likely chance speaks for it first, and the Record page counts each leg once, with the books’ chance beside ours. Each leg is also graded on its own line now: a leg could take the result of the same player’s bet at another line.

entries.title: The Parlays page makes way for the game report parlays
entries.body: The Parlays page is gone from every league. Each game’s three-leg parlays and scorer pairs are on its game report and on the Report Picks page, graded on the Record page under “The Game Report Picks and Parlays”. The two-leg Edge and Most Likely parlays are no longer built; their record stays on the Record page, marked retired. An old Parlays link opens Report Picks.

entries.title: No empty duplicate NFL players in search
entries.body: Searching an NFL name could list the player twice: once by name, and once by a short form like “J.Brissett” that opened an empty card. The short forms come from the play-by-play file and are no longer listed; the player’s own entry has all the numbers.

entries.title: Player search is fast again
entries.body: Searching for a player took seconds, up to 15 for a college football name, and every letter you typed sent its own search, so the answer to the name you meant came last. Each league’s names are now kept ready, a search answers in a fraction of a second, and the page asks once you pause typing, showing “Searching” while it does. A name we hold no longer comes with a list of near spellings; those show only when nobody has the name as typed.

entries.title: Search finds the player you typed
entries.body: Type a player’s name on the Players page and that player’s page opens, even when tonight’s board prices someone with a similar name. Before, a near name on tonight’s board stopped the search there: “jacoby brissett” showed Jacob Rodriguez as the closest match. Now, when the board can only guess at the name, the whole league is searched too, and a player found by the name typed comes first. A misspelling finds the nearest name, whether or not that player is on tonight’s board.

entries.title: A college game filed twice shows once
entries.body: Some college football games are stored more than once for a player: the box score’s line beside the play-by-play’s, a copy a day off, or a copy under ESPN’s team number. A player’s game log, their page and its league ranks now read those copies as one game, each part of the box score taken from the fuller line, so a quarterback no longer shows 0 of 9 for 0 yards beside the 19 of 31 for 260 they threw that day, and no game counts twice toward a rank.

entries.title: A game still waiting on its box score is not a game of zeros
entries.body: The game log counted a game whose box score had not landed yet as a game played, a row of dashes that dragged a player’s averages down. On the live file, Joe Burrow’s Sunday game put his average at 265 passing yards a game instead of 298. That game now says its box score is not in yet, in the game log and on the player’s page, and it stays out of games played, totals and averages until its line arrives.

entries.title: A full page for every player
entries.body: Open any player, in any league we keep box scores for, and the Players page becomes that player’s page. A header in the club’s colours carries the headshot, the name, the club, number and position, and the height, weight and age. Under it are six menus. Overview leads with the season’s four numbers and where each ranks in the league, then the previous game with both records, a splits table, the last five games, the latest news and tonight’s markets. News holds the roster’s latest injury note, any move between clubs and the headlines that name the player or the club. Stats goes season by season, Bio lists the roster’s facts, Splits breaks the season down by venue, result, month and opponent, and Game Log is the full game log. Ranks count only players with enough games or volume, so a one-game wonder never leads a rate. ESPN’s QBR isn’t in our files, so quarterbacks show the passer rating instead.

entries.title: A game log for every player
entries.body: Every player’s page has a Game log button. It opens their whole season, one line per game, newest first: the opponent, the result and the score, then their stats laid out like a box score. That means passing, rushing and receiving in football; the full box in basketball; a skater’s or a goalie’s line in hockey; and a hitter’s or a pitcher’s line in baseball. Season totals and per-game averages are underneath, with a season picker where we have more than one. It covers the NFL, college football, the NBA, the WNBA, college basketball, the NHL and MLB.

entries.title: Report Picks, in three tabs, with its own record
entries.body: The Report Picks page now opens in three tabs. Today’s picks shows what the day carries, and how the finished games’ picks and parlays went, then every game as a card you can open: live games first, then the ones still to play, then the finished ones with their result. Record shows how every pick and parlay from our game reports has done, with each leg marked. How our reports did fact-checks every finished game’s report.

entries.title: The Game Report Picks and Parlays
entries.body: The Record page has one section for everything our game reports bet. It covers every pick, split into player props, touchdown picks (goal-scorer picks in hockey) and game bets, and every three-leg parlay and touchdown or scorer pair, with how often each leg hits. Pick a league for its own, or All for every league side by side. It sits near the top of the page.

entries.title: Your place stays put when you leave the app
entries.body: Open a section, like a game report’s “Parlays for this game”, leave the app and come back, and the section closed and the page jumped. Coming back redraws the page with what changed, and a new version of the site or the phone itself can reload it. Now every section you open stays open through a redraw, and the page keeps your spot. When you come back to the same page within two hours, even after a reload, your sections open again and the page scrolls back to where you were.

entries.title: Every league’s game parlays, on its record
entries.body: The Record page now keeps the record of the parlays our game reports post, league by league. Pick a league and “Parlays for this game” shows its three-leg parlays and its touchdown or scorer pairs. For each, you see how many tickets hit and what they made at one unit a ticket, and how many legs hit, each beside the chance we gave them. It also shows the legs by market, how many losing tickets missed by a single leg, and the newest tickets with every leg marked and what the player did. “All” shows every league in one table.

entries.title: Every read says how its kind has done
entries.body: Each section of a game report now opens with how that kind of read has done on finished games, for example “Our matchup reads so far: 43 of 73 right (59%).” A finished prop says our number beside theirs (“Won · 31 points (our number 26.4)”). The Record page adds how often our number was nearer what happened than the book’s line, and shows “How our reports did” for every league, open to everyone.

entries.title: How sure we were, and how often it held
entries.body: “How our reports did” on the Report Picks page now checks our percentages too. For each band of how sure the call on who wins was (50–60%, 60–70%, and up), it shows how many of those games the side we picked actually won, with our team ratings’ own pick beside it. A side we give 70% should win about seven times in ten, and now you can see whether it does.

entries.title: Every finished game’s report checks its own facts
entries.body: After a game, its report now checks everything it told you before it, not just its reads: what the spread and total said against the final (who covered, over or under), our ratings’ and our simulation’s picks, whether the game went the way the report said it would, whether everyone on the injury report played and which regulars sat that we never listed, and who scored among the players we gave a touchdown chance. A read that missed says why when a player’s minutes were far off their own, and each report lists its best calls and biggest misses. Every finished game’s check is listed under “How our reports did” on the Report Picks page, with the totals, the misses included.

entries.title: Go back to any game and see if we were right
entries.body: Every finished game’s graded report is now kept for good, with its parlays, its picks and how each one did. Open any past game from a team’s schedule and our report on it is there under the score: every read marked right or wrong, every pick and parlay leg won or lost, and how the report did on top.

entries.title: A finished game’s report says what it got right
entries.body: Once a game is over, its report grades itself against the box score. Every matchup read, breakout candidate, fade, starting pitcher and goalie is marked right or wrong on the stat it points to, against the player’s own average (“Right: 31 points, above the 26 average over the last 10 games”). Every offense against defense call is marked too: the run game, what a defense was said to give up, basketball’s key matchups and hockey’s shots. The report opens on how it did, and the game’s parlays and picks now stay on its page after the start, each saying whether it won.

entries.title: A finished game keeps its report’s picks
entries.body: Once a game starts, the boards take its picks down, and its report was being written again without them, so a finished game’s report could lose its “Our picks” card and its reads’ picks, and Report Picks could lose the game. College basketball’s finished games lost their reports altogether. Each game now keeps the report it had right before it started, picks and reads and all, marked “as written before the game started”, so every finished game has our picks to grade.

entries.title: First-scorer long shots show their results
entries.body: On a finished game, first touchdown and first basket long shots showed no result: they carry the name of their game, and the page took that to mean a game bet like a moneyline. Only real game bets are read that way now, so these picks say whether they won, with the number, like every other pick.

entries.title: Report picks, with their own page and record
entries.body: A new Report Picks page lists every bet our game reports post, game by game: each report’s picks, its matchup reads’ picks, and its breakout candidates and fades, with the price and our chance, then the game’s three-leg parlays and pairs. The Record page has a Report bets section for each sport showing how those picks and parlays have done, counted on their own. The same picks also sit in the Most Likely and Edge books, so they’re never added into those totals.

entries.title: NFL games show their results too
entries.body: When finished games started showing how every pick did, the NFL board was left out: its file never says which sport it is, so the results step skipped it. The NFL’s finished games now show their results like every other league’s.

entries.title: Did the go-to scorer score?
entries.body: Each football report names every team’s go-to scorer, the player our touchdown numbers make the likeliest to score. Once the game is over, that line now says whether they did: “Scored”, “Scored 2”, “Didn’t score” or “Didn’t play”, from the record’s own grading of the box score.

entries.title: Results on the Tonight tab and the Pick of the Day
entries.body: Once a pick’s game is over, its row on the Tonight tab and the Pick of the Day card now show how it did, the same way the game page does: “Won · 7 receptions”, “Lost · didn’t score”, or void when the player didn’t play.

entries.title: A finished UFC fight shows how our bet did
entries.body: Once a fight on the UFC tab is over, its card now says how it ended (“Alex Pereira won by KO/TKO at 3:10 of round 2”, “won by decision”, or no winner for a draw or a no contest) and whether our bet won or lost: the moneyline, the method, a finish, the distance, the rounds or the exact round, graded by the same rules as the bet-slip checker. A draw or a no contest voids the bet. The fight report’s call says whether it was right.

entries.title: A finished game shows how every pick did
entries.body: When a game is over, its page now opens on the final score and how we did: our picks won and lost, the parlays and scorer pairs that hit, and whether our call on who wins was right. Every pick card shows its result with the real number (“Won · 4 rebounds”, “Lost · didn’t score”). The game report marks each pick, each breakout and fade pick, every parlay leg and ticket, and its call. The Parlays page marks each finished game’s tickets. Results come from the record’s own grading of the box score, in every league.

entries.title: A written report for every UFC fight
entries.body: Every fight on the UFC tab now has a written report under its card, laid out like the game reports. It covers who we think wins (the price’s call, with our fight model’s chance beside it), and the case for each fighter from the card’s measured numbers: style, striking, takedowns, submissions, age and red flags. Then the fighters side by side, how the fight ends (knockout, submission or decision, and how long it should go), weigh-ins and the venue, our bet or why there’s none, and what would void it.

entries.title: Our record sets the bar for one-team parlays
entries.body: A game’s parlay or touchdown pair with all one team’s players has to be clearly the stronger read before we post it: 4 points likelier than the best ticket with both teams, or 3 research points stronger for a pair. That bar is now set by our own record. After each grading pass, the box compares how often one-team and two-team tickets hit against the chance they were posted at. If one-team tickets fall short more, the bar goes up; if they do better, it comes down. It waits for 30 graded tickets of each kind and stays between 2 and 10 points.

entries.title: A touchdown flashes on the live score
entries.body: When a touchdown happens while you have a live NFL or college football game open, the scoring team’s score pulses gold and a TOUCHDOWN tag covers its name for a few seconds, at the top of the page and in the bar that stays when you scroll. It shows only for a touchdown you see happen: not when you open or come back to the game, not for a field goal, and never on a game you saved for later. On a TV delay it flashes when your TV shows it.

entries.title: Our ratings’ pick, beside the call
entries.body: Every game report’s “Who we think wins” now shows our own team ratings’ pick under the call, tagged Unproven, and says when they pick the other team. The line beside it says why it’s unproven: in the NFL our ratings’ disagreements with the closing line have carried nothing, in MLB bets on them alone lost 12.4%, and elsewhere what we’ve measured. The call itself still follows the price.

entries.title: Who we think wins, in every game report
entries.body: Every game report now has a “Who we think wins” section under our picks. It gives the team, its chance to win and how sure we are (a clear favorite, favored, a lean or a coin flip), with a bar for both sides. Under that are the numbers behind the chance and the case for each team from the report’s own data: each offense against the other defense, the records, the last five games, home and road, who is out, the starting pitchers and the goalies. When more of the report points to the underdog, it says that’s the case for an upset. The chance comes from the books’ moneyline with their cut taken out, else the spread, else our simulation, because our team ratings alone have not beaten the price.

entries.title: Parlays take both sides of the game
entries.body: Each game’s three-leg parlays and touchdown pairs could all go to one team when that team’s legs were a point or two likelier. Now a ticket whose legs are all one team’s is posted only when it’s clearly the stronger read than the best ticket with both teams: 4 points likelier for a parlay, 3 research points stronger for a touchdown pair. At most one of a game’s tickets can be one team’s while a two-team ticket fits. When the other team has nothing good enough, the game posts what it has. Every one-team ticket says which it was.

entries.title: Each team’s timeouts left
entries.body: A live football game now shows each team’s timeouts left as three bars, lit for each one it has: under the team’s name and record at the top of the page, and under its logo in the bar that stays at the top when you scroll. Overtime shows two in the NFL and one in college. When the live feed doesn’t give the count, no bars show.

entries.title: The field under the score, in 3D
entries.body: A live football game’s field under the score is now drawn in 3D: mown turf, each club’s end zone in its colour with its name, the yard lines and numbers, the home club’s logo at midfield, the blue line of scrimmage, the yellow line to gain, the drive as a ribbon in the offence’s colour and the ball on the line. The goal posts stand straight up, two yards behind each end line, with the crossbar ten feet up over it, because the posts and the grass are drawn by the same camera.

entries.title: The newest play on top
entries.body: A football game’s play-by-play put its drives newest first, but the plays inside each drive ran forwards, so the play just run sat at the bottom of the top drive. Every play now reads newest first, inside each drive too: in the list beside the live game, on the Plays tab and in the last few plays on each Live tab card. Each drive’s heading still names its key play and the score it left.

entries.title: No score before a game starts
entries.body: The strip of games across the top of the live page showed 0–0 for games that hadn’t started yet. The score feed fills in a 0 before the game begins, and the strip printed it. Now a game shows its score only once it’s live or over. Before that, its chip has the start time and the two teams. The same zeros are gone from the scoreboard pictures before first pitch or kickoff, the arena boards before the tip or puck drop, the second screen and the game chat’s header.

entries.title: One field on the live football page
entries.body: The stadium picture with the play drawn on it, and the field-position strip under it, are gone from a live football game. The strip under the score is the page’s one field: where the ball is, the line to gain and the drive. The Last play card says the play in words, with the people in it.

entries.title: The touchdown rule reads the real red-zone share
entries.body: A Most Likely touchdown pick needs a 45% chance, or 40% when the player has 30% of their team’s red-zone work. That 30% has been an estimate of their chances this week. From Monday night’s game it is their measured share of their team’s carries and targets inside the 20 over their last games, counted from the play-by-play, and the pick says which it read. What moves on the board: a player whose estimate and real share differ can enter or leave Most Likely’s touchdown picks between 40% and 45%. The bars are unchanged.

entries.title: The live game page, without the field and in reading order
entries.body: A live football game’s Last play card no longer draws a field: it says the play in words, with the people in it and their game so far. The page now reads top to bottom: the score and where the ball is; the play right now (the picture, the words, the win chance), above the tabs so no tab hides it; your bets on the game; Call it and the chat; then the tabs, with Play-By-Play as the game so far, drive by drive.

entries.title: Each team’s form in the basketball and hockey reports
entries.body: Every NBA, college basketball and WNBA report’s “How the game should go”, and every NHL report’s matchup, now opens with each side’s form: its record over its last ten games this season and how much it outscored teams by, then the home side’s record at home and the visitors’ on the road. Only this season’s final scores count. Baseball’s game facts say the same form line from opening day.

entries.title: Pace in the basketball report reads per 48 minutes
entries.body: The report’s new “How the game should go” said each team’s pace as “possessions a game”. Pace is counted per 48 minutes, as the tape’s pace row on the same page says, so on a 40-minute college game it read about a fifth more possessions than a college team really has. It now says “per 48 minutes”, the same number as the tape, and a college game’s averages are Division I’s rather than “the league’s”.

entries.title: Each pick says the main way it loses
entries.body: Every pick on a game report’s card now ends with the strongest reason against it from the player’s matchup read, such as the pass rush they face, so you can weigh the risk before you bet.

entries.title: Hockey reports: the lines and the last meeting
entries.body: NHL game reports now show each team’s top two forward lines and top defense pair, with how often they have played together and who they are built without tonight. They also show the last meeting between the two teams, with the score and who scored.

entries.title: Basketball reports: the absences, the pace, the last meeting
entries.body: NBA, college and WNBA game reports now say what each absence changes: the minutes and points a ruled-out player leaves, and who took their share of the points in the games they missed. They also cover how the game should go (both teams’ pace and the total against the league’s average game) and the last meeting, with who each side played without that night.

entries.title: Breakout candidates and fades on every game
entries.body: Every game report, in every sport, now lists its breakout candidates and its fades. The strongest case comes first. Each player gets up to four measured reasons (their role and where it is moving, what the defense gives up to them, the game around them), their recent form, their pick where the board has one, and the main way the pick loses.

entries.title: A player’s season beside their last six games
entries.body: The game report’s red-zone counts, the likeliest scorer and a scorer’s pick card now give a player’s whole season beside their last six games: their carries and targets inside the 20, their carries inside the 5 and their targets inside the 10.

entries.title: The fixed NBA rotation check runs first tonight
entries.body: Yesterday we said Saturday night’s model refit would re-run the NBA’s fixed rotation check. It ran other work first and stopped with most of its time unused, so the check did not run and the three rotation adjustments stayed off. A check whose code changed now runs first, and a refit spends the time it has left on the next piece of work that fits.

entries.title: Why the likeliest scorer, in our numbers
entries.body: Each team’s likeliest scorer in the game reports is picked by our touchdown model: their share of the work, their red-zone touches, their touchdowns and what the defense gives up to their position. The line now says that evidence instead of only the points the books expect their team to score. It gives our chance beside the chance their price implies, their touchdowns this season, their carries and targets inside the 20 with their share of their team’s, and how many touchdowns this defense allows to their position.

entries.title: The red zone says the real counts
entries.body: The red zone section of each NFL game report now says who gets the ball inside the 20 in real numbers, not our estimate. For each player it lists their carries and targets inside the 20 in their last six games, with the ones inside the 5 and the 10 called out, how many that is a game, and their share of their team’s. Then it says about how many to expect in this game against this defense: their rate times how many plays inside the 20 the defense allows compared with an average defense. The team line gives the same for the whole offense.

entries.title: Every live play says who did what
entries.body: The live football play-by-play now says each play the way a broadcaster would. The card at the top opens on the down and where the ball was, then who did what, where it went and what it changed: “On 3rd & 9 from the DET 44, Jared Goff throws deep right to Jameson Williams for a 56-yard touchdown. Lions 7, Patriots 3.” Every row in the play list reads the same way, with the players in bold: who made the sack, who broke up the pass, the gap a run went through, and a flag’s foul and the player it was on (“False start on Kayshon Boutte, 5 yds”) instead of “Penalty on the offense”. First downs and turnovers on downs are called out, kickoffs are drawn from the kicking team’s side of the field, and the list beside the page no longer cuts plays off.

entries.title: The live page says each thing once
entries.body: The live football page no longer says the same thing twice. While the game is on, the drive chart is gone, because the field under the score shows the drive. The drive card now opens on the last play and leaves the down and the spot to that field, and the bar at the top of the screen says them under the clock once you scroll. The win chance shows once, in its own card, and the photograph no longer repeats where the ball is. On a computer, the column beside the Play-By-Play tab shows our picks on the game instead of a second list of the plays. And the plays name their players again: most passes in an NFL game had lost the passer and the receiver, so a 56-yard touchdown read “The Lions for a 56-yard touchdown.”

entries.title: Bet a whole parlay from its card
entries.body: Every parlay and touchdown pair in the game reports and on the Parlays page now has a Bet it button. At a sportsbook whose links can carry the whole ticket, one tap puts every leg on your bet slip. At a book that takes one bet per link, you add the legs one at a time and they stack on the same slip as a parlay. You can also open any other book and key it in. A same-game parlay is priced by the book, and it pays less than the legs’ own prices multiplied, so check the price before you place it.

entries.title: Every game report opens on our picks
entries.body: Every game report now opens on our picks for that game, ranked best to worst, the way a researcher would hand them to you. Each pick shows its book and price, our chance, its fair price and the most we’d pay for it (never past −250), how often the player has cleared that number this season and in their last five games, the matchup and role behind it, and how that kind of pick has hit, both on our board and in our hand-researched picks. Then comes the game’s best parlay and its touchdown pair. When nothing on a game clears our bars, the report says so and names the two closest picks and what holds each one back.

entries.title: A way back on every page a link opens
entries.body: Every page you reach by tapping something on another page now has a Back at its top that names where it goes: “← Back to the game”, “← Back to Most Likely”, “← Back to the Lions”, “← Back to the search”. It works like your phone’s back-swipe. You land where you were, scrolled to the same spot, and going back to the player search brings back what you typed. A player’s teammate or a team’s opponent opens as its own page, so Back steps through each one. Pages you open from the menu or the tab bar don’t get one, because the menu is the way around. The game, pick and play-by-play pages keep their own Back, and when you come back to a game from a player its report named, the game’s Back still goes where you first opened it from.

entries.title: The angles say each team right
entries.body: The angles in the NFL game reports put a team’s nickname into sentences written for its abbreviation, so they read “Lions gives up”, “Lions’s coverage” and “Patriots runs on 55% of its red-zone plays”. They now read like the rest of the report: “the Lions give up”, “the Lions’ coverage”, “the Lions blitz”, “against the Lions in their last 3 games” and “The Patriots run on 55% of their red-zone plays”, while a school stays singular (“Indiana gives up … its”). The red-zone lines now give the player’s full name (“Rhamondre Stevenson”, not “R.Stevenson”), and a player on the injury report is skipped for the next man.

entries.title: A shorter, cleaner game report
entries.body: The game report now opens on the short version alone. Every other section folds to its title, one tap away, and a button opens them all at once. How the units rank is now a chart: each offense against the defense it faces on passing, rushing, pressure and the red zone, as bars where longer is better, colored green in the league’s top third and red in its bottom third. The tables with every number fold underneath, and copying the report still copies all of it.

entries.title: Picks we oversell go on paper
entries.body: A kind of pick whose record says it claims far more than it hits is no longer posted. It is still recorded and graded on paper, and it comes back on its own once thirty of its paper picks run honest. First on paper: Most Likely picks 15 or more points above the books’ price, which said 76% and hit 36% on our NFL board. After every settle, our record checks each league’s Most Likely picks by market and by how far they sat above the price, and puts any kind that ran 10 or more points hot on paper. The Edge boards now record the picks our record turns down, so those can come back too. And a matchup pick whose chance our record correction lowers under its 55% bar now comes off instead of staying posted.

entries.title: The game report’s numbers in green and red
entries.body: The game reports now color their numbers, not just their names. Every rank in a sentence is green in the league’s top third and red in its bottom third, like the Packers’ passing game (4th in the league) against the Lions’ pass defense (22nd). What a defense gives up is colored for that defense, so “gives up the second-most points” is red. A last game’s win is green and a loss red, and so are a goalie’s form against expected goals, a lineup against tonight’s pitcher’s hand, the red zone’s numbers against an average team, and rest: a rested team or the rest edge green, the second night of a back-to-back or a tired bullpen red. A rank with no good or bad side, like the most plays run, stays plain. The key at the top says it once: green is good for the team or player it’s about, so a red number on a defense is good news for the offense facing it.

entries.title: The game page in plain words
entries.body: The game page’s notes now read as sentences. Where the money is going says who the traders are and gives its time in Eastern time. Where the line opened gives the day it was first priced and which way the spread and total moved since. Every weather line, on the game page, the pick cards and the reports, says what a forecast like this one has done, such as receiving yards running 3% lower than in calm games. The weather’s effect on each pick is unchanged.

entries.title: Game reports you can read at a glance
entries.body: Every player with a matchup read is now colored wherever the report names them: green for a breakout candidate or a favorable matchup, red for an unfavorable one. The tables color each rank by where it stands in the league, the injury list colors out and questionable, each line’s lead-in is bold, and one key at the top says what the colors mean. A few lines that read badly are clearer too, like the weakest cornerback now named once instead of twice.

entries.title: The game chat bar stays at the bottom
entries.body: On an iPhone, the game chat bar could get stuck halfway up the game page, with the top bar and the menu’s dots moved up too, until the page was scrolled. Closing the chat, or sending a message, took its typing box away while the keyboard was up, and the phone never said so. The chat now lets go of the box first, the site puts every pinned bar back whenever the screen and the page disagree, and the chat bar steps aside while you type anywhere else.

entries.title: Who gets the ball, in color
entries.body: In the game reports, the lines that say who gets the ball now color each player’s name by the matchup in that game: green for a breakout candidate or a favorable matchup, red for an unfavorable one. That covers who gets the targets, who carries it and who gets the chances inside the 20 in football, and who carries each team in basketball. A key sits under the section’s title, and a tap on a name opens the player’s page.

entries.title: Most Likely picks follow our betting rules
entries.body: A Most Likely pick that breaks one of our rules now tops out at Worth a look, and its card says which rule. The rules include a rushing over on a team expected to trail, a reception over from a player outside their team’s top two targets with little volume, and a quarterback rushing under. Touchdown picks are checked against 45%, or 40% with a big red-zone role. Game reports add four game scripts with the picks that hold up in most of them, each team’s touchdown chances ranked beside what the defense allows, and the price to take every pick at.

entries.title: The UFC record shows UFC’s fights
entries.body: The Record page’s UFC tab showed 0-0-0 although 43 fight picks were recorded, because it read the edge picks’ book, which UFC never uses. It now leads with UFC’s own fight picks: the record, the profit calendar and every settled fight, still kept out of the All bets total. The “This week” card now follows the tab you’re on, so the UFC tab no longer shows NBA and NFL picks.

entries.title: The game reports read in plain words
entries.body: Every league’s game report was rewritten in plainer words. A rank is said from its near end (“the eighth-best rate in the league”, not “23rd of 32, 1st the stingiest”), a number close to the league is “about average” instead of “0% below”, “the 1st-most” is “the most”, and terms like “in the box” and goals saved above expected are written out.

entries.title: A total moving against the money is said
entries.body: A game report already said when the spread moved toward the side with the minority of the money. It now says the same for the total, for example a total falling from 43.5 to 40.5 while 70% of the prediction-market money sat on the over.

entries.title: College props grade on ESPN’s box score
entries.body: College props now grade on ESPN’s final box score, the one the books settle on. When the official stat file lands days later, its numbers no longer overwrite the box score’s, so a bet graded that night stands. A game is no longer stored twice once both have landed.

entries.title: A lead running back is never marked avoid
entries.body: A back with 40% or more of their team’s carries can read as a tough matchup, but never as one to avoid. That rule used to apply only at 55% of the carries, while a receiver counted as featured at 18% of the targets.

entries.title: A matchup read’s pick needs the numbers behind it
entries.body: A breakout or good-matchup read gets its over, and a tough one its under, only when our number on that side is 55% or better and the books’ price doesn’t argue against it. A read alone is never a bet. Where the numbers don’t back a pick, the card says why: a coin flip, our number against the read, or our number too far from every book. On the NFL board a read pick under 60% is held back, and the card says so.

entries.title: Every matchup read gets its pick on its side
entries.body: A player the matchup scan calls a breakout candidate or a good matchup now carries an over on their card, and one it says could struggle carries an under, whenever our number on that side is at least even. Before, a read got a pick only when that side cleared the Most Likely bar (60% for NFL props), and unders almost never did, so many cards read “No Most Likely pick”. Under 60% in the NFL it rides as the read’s own matchup pick, tracked on paper, and the board keeps its bar. Where our number has the read’s side losing more often than not, the card now says our number disagrees. The game report’s player cards name each read’s pick too.

entries.title: Touchdown pairs are chosen on our research
entries.body: Each game’s touchdown pairs used to be its likeliest priced scorers. Now a football scorer is a leg only when our research makes a case for them: their team’s expected points, the defence they face at their position, their share of the work, their red-zone chances and trips, the matchup read (a breakout candidate counts most) and the game script (a back on a favourite, a receiver in a shootout). Every leg needs a red-zone role. Pairs are ranked on that research first and our chance second, and each leg shows its research score and the reasons behind it.

entries.title: No tackle or kicker legs on any parlay
entries.body: No parlay the site builds or suggests carries a tackle, sack or kicking prop anymore: not the game reports’ parlays, the two-leg tickets, the parlay screen, or the builder’s “stacks well with”. Those props stay on the boards as single picks.

entries.title: Polymarket's trades are read again
entries.body: Polymarket retired the service its trade history came from on 2 November. Since then a game page's money split showed Kalshi's trades only, and the prediction-market flow feed was stuck on trades from 2 November. Both read Polymarket's new service now.

entries.title: Four parlays a game, from every prop we price
entries.body: A game's three-leg parlays were built only from the picks the board posts, about six a game in the NFL, so most games got one ticket instead of four. They now draw on every prop we price at a real book with our chance at 60% or better, nothing priced past -250 and nobody ruled out. Every ticket is still tracked and never staked.

entries.title: Bets are never graded on a box score read mid-game
entries.body: The same-night settle could file a game's box score from a copy saved while the game was being played, when a fresh read failed. A Miami receiver's Notre Dame game was filed at 75 and 92 yards against a final 144. A box score that doesn't say its game is over is never filed now, and bets graded on those copies are re-graded when the official stats land.

entries.title: More parlays a game, priced the same honest way
entries.body: A game's three-leg parlays never paired a running back with their own team's receiver, because one wants their team ahead and the other wants it chasing. That left most NFL games with one ticket instead of four. They can share a ticket now, priced as unrelated, and the ticket says it wants a close game. Legs that truly can't both hit, like an over on scoring with an under, are still never paired.

entries.title: The money split asks Polymarket the way it requires
entries.body: A game page's "where the money is going" bars were reading Kalshi's trades alone in every league: Polymarket refused every request for its trades. They now ask the way Polymarket requires for a page that size, and if it still refuses, the board says why.

entries.title: Game bets obey the record's closures
entries.body: When a slice of bets keeps landing below what we claimed, the record closes it, and a market that has lost over its whole record stops being staked. Player props and college football's game plays obeyed both; NFL, MLB and NHL spreads, totals and moneylines never checked. They do now: a game bet in a closed slice is shown with the reason and not staked.

entries.title: College basketball buys the games with player props
entries.body: College basketball's board showed no player picks: of the eight games it bought prices for on Saturday, the books posted player props on one. It bought a ranked or power school's game against a small school first, and the books don't post players there. It now buys first the games where both teams are ranked or in a power conference, like LSU at Gonzaga.

entries.title: A college player who left is read at their new school only
entries.body: College's board placed last season's players on their old school's side: a quarterback now at Rutgers was read in Boston College's game report, and graduates were priced off last year's games. Each player is now read only where this season's games and rosters put them.

entries.title: College games are filed once
entries.body: A college player's game could be stored two or three times, sometimes with different numbers, which doubled games in their log and hit rates and could void a bet. Each game is now filed once; the copies already stored are removed with one command on our side.

entries.title: College reads count the opponent, not a player's own team
entries.body: A college matchup read counted a back's own run game and their own line against them, though they are in every number they have. They are now said, not counted. A receiver who threw one trick-play pass is no longer read as a quarterback.

entries.title: A started college game keeps its pregame line
entries.body: A college board built during a game read that game's in-play line as its pregame line, so a read could say a team was expected to score 0. A game under way now keeps the last line it had before kickoff.

entries.title: One reason no longer makes a workhorse unfavorable
entries.body: A matchup read called Duke's Nate Sheppard unfavorable at Miami on one reason, Miami's run defense ranked 5th; he scored and ran for 63 yards by the second quarter. A read now needs as many reasons to lean tough as to lean good, in every sport, and a featured player (a workhorse back, a top target, a starter) needs one more. One reason against a featured player reads neutral, with the reason shown. A go-to scorer with a tough read says "tough for yards — still the go-to scorer".

entries.title: The Pick of the Day page shows its logos
entries.body: The college cards showed a grey "NCAA" text box and a college pick showed its school as letters ("RIC", "RICE vs TULN"), because that page loads no league's board. Each card now carries its teams' logos and names, so a pick shows its school's logo and "Rice vs Tulane". College leagues show their sport's ball. A moneyline reads "Rice Moneyline", not "RICE ML Moneyline", and the board's best bet shows the player's face or the team's logo. A league whose season is over no longer shows a "No pick today" card.

entries.title: A rematch shows the first game and what changed
entries.body: When two NFL teams meet for the second time in a season, the game report's "When they last met" section now shows what each side's key players did in the first game, from their own game logs, and what has changed since: a different starting quarterback, the players now on a reserve list, and the move to the other team's field.

entries.title: Player cards show the game log and the hit rate
entries.body: Each key player's card in a football game report now shows their season game by game, and for each number the board posts on them, how many of their games this season cleared it and how many of their last five ("Over 46.5 receiving yards: 4 of 6 games this season, 4 of the last 5").

entries.title: NFL reports open on the angles
entries.body: Every NFL game report now opens on "The angles": where each defense leaks to the players the other side has. It covers the top receiver against what that defense has given the top receiver it faced each week, the tight end against its tight-end coverage and the touchdowns it allows, a running quarterback against its blitz (this season, lately and in the teams' own meeting, their scrambles a game, and what the last quarterbacks ran for against it), and the red-zone scorer with their share of the touches. Each angle names the market it points at, and a defense that holds a position down is listed under "Where to be careful".

entries.title: Game reports read this season's facts
entries.body: A report could name a player on injured reserve as a team's pass rusher, miss a cornerback's coverage numbers because two sources spell their name differently, carry ESPN's leftover "questionable" after a team's final report had dropped it, and say last season's coverage numbers as if they were this season's. Players on a reserve list are now read off the roster (never named as starters, and listed with what they had this season), a defender spelled two ways is matched, a team's filed report outranks ESPN's leftover tags, and this season's numbers come first, last season's labelled as last season's.

entries.title: Every game gets its own parlays
entries.body: Every game now has four three-leg parlays and, in football, three two-leg touchdown parlays (goal-scorer pairs in hockey), built from the picks the board already posts. No two legs conflict: no player twice, no quarterback against their own receiver, no two legs that need the game to go opposite ways. Each ticket shows our chance, the fair price and the price to take it at, the game script it needs, a backup for every leg and its caveats, and each leg says why — for a scorer, their red-zone work, what the defense gives up to their position, the weather and their team's expected points. They are in every game report and on the Parlays page, now open for hockey and the WNBA too. Every ticket is graded on the record and staked at nothing until same-game parlays prove they pay.

entries.title: Matchup reads count each factor once
entries.body: A matchup read could call a team's go-to scorer a bad matchup on one defensive rank — Duke's back, with 17 touchdowns, read unfavorable at Miami because Miami's run defense ranks 5th. Every league's read counted two or three numbers about the same defense as separate reasons, and college's never heard the lines. Now a factor counts once however many of its numbers agree, a featured player can read tough but never one to avoid, college's read counts the points the lines expect, and a tough matchup for a team's likeliest scorer says so: "Unfavorable for yards — still the go-to scorer", with their touchdowns and our chance, and the report's short version names each side's likeliest scorer. Some Most Likely picks change sides with their reads; no chance changes.

entries.title: Game reports no longer tout a player who won't play
entries.body: A game report could list a ruled-out player under "Who could have a big day" and "Could shine" — in every sport. Now a player who is out, doubtful, suspended, or whose props every book has taken down gets no mention; one listed questionable or a game-time decision keeps their card but wears a Questionable mark and is kept out of the short version; and a player who missed their team's last game with nothing on the injury report is flagged too, so the game is never summed up through someone who may sit.

entries.title: Basketball and hockey picks read their own record
entries.body: Our NBA Edge picks had claimed 51.9% and landed 44.9% over 227 settled, and the board never applied the correction our other boards apply for exactly that: how our own picks have landed against what we said. The NBA, WNBA, college basketball and NHL Edge boards apply it now, each by its own record. What moves on the board: where a league's correction is in force, its Edge picks show smaller chances, edges and stakes, and fewer qualify. Most Likely is unchanged.

entries.title: The NBA's rotation rules are judged on finished seasons
entries.body: Three NBA adjustments (a player's first games back, a role that jumped, a regular's return) were switched off on Saturday morning by the model's own weekly check, which had started judging the first few weeks of this season beside two full ones. A season still being played is shown in that check now and never decides it; tonight's refit runs it again before the NBA's numbers are fitted.

entries.title: Polymarket's prices reach more college games
entries.body: Polymarket refused college basketball's two larger requests because they were not asked for a compressed answer, so only 19 of Saturday's 71 games carried its price. Every request asks that way now.

entries.title: The Lab draws again
entries.body: Since late August the Lab showed "Sorry — part of this page failed to draw" on every visit: it read each game-line replay's count under a name the replay never wrote, and the error took every league's section with it. It draws now, the game lines included, and a league whose replay cannot be drawn says so without blanking the others.

entries.title: College basketball has its own address
entries.body: qellysbook.com/cbb opens the college basketball board, as qellysbook.com/nba opens the NBA's. Every other league's board already had an address of its own.

entries.title: College's Parlays page builds
entries.body: College basketball's Parlays page said "No parlays on this board yet" every night: the two-leg builder never ran for college. It builds from college's own Edge and Most Likely picks now. College is still on probation, so every parlay is tracked and graded, and none is staked, as its singles are not.

entries.title: The scout on college cards
entries.body: College picks now carry the scout's cautions, measured on five college seasons rather than borrowed from the NBA: an under while a regular teammate sits, an over in their first game back, a minutes drop or jump, the second of two straight days, a regular's return, a player barely into their season. Each caution says what college's seasons measured. A projected blowout or shootout warns on NBA cards but not on college's: college's own seasons refused them.

entries.title: Small schools by name on college game pages
entries.body: A college game against a school below Division I named that school by an internal code ("espn:124942" for Mary Baldwin) on the game page, its scoreboard strip, the live card and the plays. They show the school's own abbreviation now.

entries.title: The Play feed opens, and college plays read their halves
entries.body: Tapping Play feed on the Live tab threw an error and scrambled the page, in every league: the button was being read as a league chip. It opens now. A college game's plays said Q2 under a card that said H2; they read H1, H2 and OT everywhere a play is timed. The feed's play cards show the player's headshot instead of their initials, and every page calls college basketball NCAAB, as the league row does.

entries.title: Every league on one row on a phone
entries.body: Adding college basketball made the league row eight across, and on phones the eighth, UFC, wrapped onto a line of its own. The leagues now share the row in equal parts, each crest sized to its share, so all eight sit on one row on every phone from a 320 to the folded iPhone Duo and the largest iPhones, with each button still a full thumb's height.

entries.title: A forecast for games abroad
entries.body: A game outside the US (London, Munich, Madrid, Mexico City, São Paulo) used to read "weather not pulled", because the National Weather Service covers the US only, so its props went without the weather. Those games now read MET Norway's forecast, in the same hourly reading at kickoff: temperature, wind and the chance of rain. US games read the NWS exactly as before. Weather data from MET Norway.

entries.title: College basketball's title futures
entries.body: College's Futures page is the NCAA tournament race's own run, two thousand seasons played out to the title: each school's projected record with its band, its chance at its conference's automatic bid and the field, and the national title, beside the books' best title price with the gap in points. A book's runner is matched to a school only by a name we have already seen; one we have not is left unpriced rather than guessed.

entries.title: The NCAA tournament race, college basketball's NBA Cup page
entries.body: College basketball's Race page plays the rest of the season out 2,000 times: every game left, each conference's tournament, the committee's selection and the bracket. Free: the field if the season ended today (68 seeded in four regions), the bubble (last four in, first four out, next four out) and every conference's race. For members: each school's chance to make the field, earn a top-four seed, reach the Sweet 16 and the Final Four and win it all, its next games at our price, its chance at its conference's automatic bid, and the games that swing the bubble. From Selection Sunday the page is the bracket itself, every result as it lands and our line on each game left. The ratings adjust for every opponent and the selection stands in for the committee; on the last three seasons it named 104 of the 110 teams the committee took at large.

entries.title: College basketball reads a player's shooting and rebounds the NBA's way
entries.body: Two reads the NBA board makes, measured on five college seasons and now on for college. Points and threes are rebuilt from a player's shot volume at their longer-run percentages instead of their last twenty games' makes (points 0.4-0.5% closer, threes 1.2-1.3%, every season held out), and rebounds and assists a minute read past their last twenty games toward their role's college average (0.5-0.8% closer). What moved on the board: a college shooter on a hot or cold run is read nearer their real percentages, and each pick shows the step and what it was measured to do.

entries.title: College basketball's shot chart and matchup view
entries.body: Every college player now has the NBA's shot chart: every shot they took, where on the floor, made or missed, drawn on the college court (a 12-foot lane and the three-point line at 22 feet 1.75 inches), game by game and for the season, by half, with their zones shaded against college basketball's own percentages. The matchup view sets their zones beside what tonight's opponent allows in each. Both open from any college prop, the way they do from an NBA prop.

entries.title: College basketball's numbers, measured on five college seasons
entries.body: We replayed every Division I box score of the last five seasons (284,087 player-games) through the college board's own projection. The minutes pieces it inherited from the WNBA held up: the starting five's news and a player's first game back each made minutes better every season, and the newest games weighted the way the WNBA's are read minutes best. Three pieces that did not hold on points in every season stay off. What moved on the board: how wide each college prop's chance is. Until the box has a month of college games to measure its own, the board had been using the NBA's starting widths, half as wide as a college player's line actually moves (points 0.30 against 0.78), which would have made every college chance too sure of itself; it now starts from college's own. The spread curve the NBA's switch turns on is college's own too: on every judged season it scored better than one width per stat in points, rebounds, assists, PRA and the three combos, and threes keep their single width, as in the NBA.

entries.title: Men's college basketball, with everything the NBA has
entries.body: College basketball has its own board: the NCAAB button, between the NBA and the WNBA. Every Division I game is on it with its lines, and player props are priced on each night's biggest games, the ranked teams and the power conferences first, where the books post them. It is the NBA's model (minutes first, then each player's rate, priced against the de-vigged market) on a 40-minute game of two halves, with Edge and Most Likely picks, the market scan, the live page with the court and the play feed, game pages, standings by conference, rosters with each school's own headshots, injuries and news. Like every new league it starts on probation: its picks are journaled and graded in public, and nothing is staked until its record earns it.

entries.title: The NBA standings show this season, not last
entries.body: The NBA Standings page was showing 2025-26's final table (Boston 56-26, Detroit 60-22) two weeks into the new season. ESPN names a winter season by the year it ends, and the page asked for the year it began. It now asks for the right one.

entries.title: Games under a retractable roof no longer take the outdoor weather
entries.body: The schedule only says whether a retractable roof was open after the game is played, so the board had been reading every coming game in Arizona, Atlanta, Dallas, Houston and Indianapolis as open air and cutting its props for the forecast wind and rain. Those roofs were shut for 9 home games in 10 from 2016 to 2025, and open only on fair days, never in rain. They now read as closed, and the game card says "Retractable roof · expected closed". This week it takes the forecast's wind and rain cut off the 49ers at the Cowboys.

entries.title: Weather does not change who scores the first touchdown
entries.body: Rain cuts a receiver's chance of scoring a touchdown at all, so we asked whether it also shifts who scores a team's first one toward the running backs. Over every team's first touchdown since 2021, it does not: in rain the pass catchers scored their usual share, and moving the first-touchdown shares by the rain cut made the predictions worse. The first-touchdown picks keep reading the game lines, which already carry the forecast, and leave the player shares alone.

entries.title: A pick's weather line says which way it cuts for that pick
entries.body: The weather line under a pick is written for the player's position, so the rain line under a running back's carries names both their carries (up, teams run more in rain) and their catches (down). It used to be marked against an over whenever any number in it fell. It is now marked by what the weather does to that pick's own market, and a market the weather leaves alone, like a back's rushing yards, says so instead of borrowing a cut that is not its own.

entries.title: Rain and wind now move a quarterback's completions and a kicker's points
entries.body: Both markets have been priced since October, and the forecast never touched them. Measured over ten seasons, the same way as the rest of the weather: a quarterback completes about 8% fewer passes in rain and 5-7% fewer in 12+ mph wind, and a kicker scores about 7% fewer points in 12+ mph wind. Both now move with the kickoff forecast, at the forecast's own chance of rain. Pass attempts, field goals made, and kickers in rain or cold showed nothing clear and stay untouched.

entries.title: The game report says why a matchup card disagrees with it
entries.body: The report names the units where a game tilts, "room to run for the Chiefs", from two seasons of play; a player's card reads this season's numbers, the lines and the forecast, and now and then leans the other way. Where a card on that side reads against the edge, the report now says why in the same sentence: "…though the Falcons give up the sixth-fewest rushing yards to running backs".

entries.title: The Status page checks the game report against the matchup cards
entries.body: After every build the board checks its own claims. It now also counts a game report that gives a side the run or pass edge while a matchup card on that side reads the other way, the contradiction a member caught on the Commanders at the Giants. The count is on the Status page; nothing on the board is changed by it.

entries.title: The game report gives this season's rank beside the two-season one
entries.body: A unit's rank in the report blends this season with last, the way it predicts best, and in November that blend can still sit far from this season alone: the Giants' run defense read 30th while ranking 13th on this season's games. Where the two sit a quarter of the league apart, the report, the game plan and the mismatch list now give both, "30th; 13th this season alone". Which edges are named, and for whom, is unchanged.

entries.title: A tough defence is said as the fewest, not the 30th-most
entries.body: The matchup line under a prop and on the fantasy page counted every defence from the top: the Giants read "189.2 passing yards a game, the 30th-most". A defence in the bottom half of the table is now counted from its own end, "the 3rd-fewest", in the sentence, its second line and the rank chip. The numbers and colours are unchanged.

entries.title: A bet you log in the evening keeps its day
entries.body: My Bets dated a bet logged after 7pm Eastern (8pm in summer) with the next day. On a Sunday evening that put it in next week, so it didn't count toward your weekly limit and the limit's warning never came. Bets now take the Eastern day, the same day your Monday-to-Sunday week is counted in. The fantasy desk shows tonight's game after 7pm too, the Record card says Today all evening, and the countdown to a league's next slate no longer drops a day.

entries.title: NBA picks count in the market-against-market closing line
entries.body: The Record page's matched closing-line figure compares the market's no-vig chance when a pick was made with its no-vig chance at the close. No NBA pick carried the first half, and NFL picks were missing the second half unless we had bought the close. NBA picks now carry the market's fair price from every book quoting their number, and NFL picks take their close from our own line snapshots, so both count from today. Grading finished picks also reads those snapshots once a pass, not three times.

entries.title: Every college game is on the board
entries.body: A college Saturday showed only 25 games: ESPN's scoreboard hands back about two dozen whatever is asked for, so evening games like Michigan and Michigan State never reached the board, the live scores or the playoff race's standings. Each conference's own scoreboard is now asked too and the games joined, so the whole FBS slate shows.

entries.title: NFL and college picks post the day before the games
entries.body: Saturday's NFL board showed Sunday's games without prices, so no Sunday picks: prices were bought only on a night a league played. The NFL's and college's boards now buy tomorrow's games the day before, so Sunday's picks are up on Saturday, Monday night's on Sunday, Thursday night's on Wednesday and college's Saturday on Friday. Tonight's games still come first. The NBA and NHL boards stay on the day: their books post player lines that day.

entries.title: Grading picks takes the server a fraction of the time
entries.body: The pass that grades finished picks read each day's box scores once for every open pick, checked every pick ever graded for corrected stats, and rewrote the whole Record page, every five minutes; its first timed run took over eighteen minutes. It now reads each day once, checks the last week (every night it still checks them all), and updates the Record page every ten minutes. No grade changes.

entries.title: Busy game days leave more of the server for the boards
entries.body: Every few minutes the server grades the picks whose games have finished, and on a game day it was also refitting six of its learning models on nearly every one of those passes, close to ten minutes of work every five. Picks still grade the moment their games end; the learning models now refit at most once an hour, and never skip a graded pick.

entries.title: The weather desk measures how sure it should be
entries.body: The weather desk is still paused. Its forecasts were right about the day but too sure about the degree: it priced every city's high as if the forecast were rarely more than two degrees off. It now measures that from its own record, each forecast it logged beside the bracket that actually won that day, and grades the calls it would make with the measured spread, out of sight, until they win about what they claim.

entries.title: The Lab's football replay fits inside its nightly hour
entries.body: The Lab's NFL numbers have been dated 29 September because the replay ran past the hour the server gives it and published nothing. It now reads its closing lines once, inside its own half hour, and starts a week only when there is time to finish it, so the NFL section is written before the hour is up.

entries.title: Leagues out of season stop rebuilding every few minutes
entries.body: Baseball's page was being rebuilt every few minutes for a slate with no games, about three minutes of the server's time out of every twenty. A league whose season is over now refreshes every six hours, and that time goes to the leagues being played and to the models' weekly refit.

entries.title: The nightly jobs run once a day, as they should
entries.body: Two of the server's background routines kept their notes in one file and could overwrite each other's, so a job that had already run that day was sometimes started again: on 7 November the model refit ran four times. Each now records only its own notes, so the nightly jobs run once and the boards keep the server to themselves for the rest of the day.

entries.title: The weekly model refit gets its share of the server
entries.body: The models' weekly refit and the weekly backtests were running at the very lowest priority on the server, behind every board rebuild, so they got about an eighth of the processor and every large fit was cut off at its time limit: the NFL's recency weights still dated from August, and the backtests had not replayed the NFL since 29 September. They were meant to run level with the board rebuilds, and now they do, with the site itself still first in line.

entries.title: The weekly model refit no longer spends nights on finished seasons
entries.body: The models re-learn each sport from its whole history a piece at a time, a little each night. On 7 November baseball and the WNBA, their seasons over, held two of the round's places while the NFL's recency weights still dated from August. A league whose season is over, with its next one more than three weeks away, now sits the round out, and the weekly backtests stop replaying it once its last games are in. It comes back three weeks before its season, so its models are fitted on everything it played before the first game is priced.

entries.title: Leagues out of season are greyed in the league row
entries.body: A league whose season is over now shows grey in the row of leagues at the top of the page, so the ones playing tonight stand out: today that is baseball and the WNBA. It is still a button and its page still opens, with everything on it; hovering over it says the season is over. A league turns grey when the season calendar says it is done, or sooner when its own scoreboard shows the last game of the postseason has been played (the same signal that stops the site buying odds for it), and turns back the day its season starts.

entries.title: Every closing line is the player's own
entries.body: A closing line is the number a bet is measured against at kickoff, and the record's closing-line value is built from them. Early in the season the odds feed could file one player's prices under another's name when the two shared a first initial and a surname and the second man's own prices were missing from that pull: Amon-Ra St. Brown's Week 1 receiving numbers were also filed under A.J. Brown, four days after A.J. Brown had played the season's opener. No close reads such a copy now, a close that came from one is read again from the player's own prices or left empty when they have none, and the feed only fills a missing price from a game it can prove is the player's. Grades and results are unchanged; only closing-line value moves, for the bets it touched.

entries.title: The models' weekly refit finishes what it starts
entries.body: The weekly refit re-learns each sport from its whole history, a piece at a time, a little each night. Last night four long jobs shared the server's one processor at once, and the refit ran out its time inside the NFL's first fit without finishing a market, though on its own that fit takes about five minutes. Two of those jobs, the refit and the Lab's replay, now take turns. A week's round of refits also used to start over every Wednesday and throw away what it had finished, so the NFL, whose turn comes about once a week, never got through; a round now runs to its end before the next begins, and a fit that makes no progress in two full runs is set aside so the rest of the sport still refits. Nothing on the board moves until those refits land.

entries.title: A back's carries go up in the rain
entries.body: Measured on ten NFL seasons: in rain, teams run more (their running backs' carries were 6.9% higher than usual, in nine seasons of ten), and a back keeps their share of them. So a back's carries now rise when rain is forecast, by the forecast's own chance: a 70% chance of rain is 70% of the step.
